subtopic: POSITION OP CANADIAN GOVERNMENT-STATEMENT OP SECRETARY OP STATE FOR EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): Mr. Speaker, in view of the many references recently made in the press to certain art treasures which were brought to Canada by the Polish authorities in 1940 and in order that there may be no misapprehension about the position of the Canadian government, I think I should give the house a rather full account of the circumstances.
On July 11, 1940, the Consul-General of Poland, Mr. Victor Podoski, informed the Secretary of State for External Affairs that the Polish ship Batory was en route to Canada carrying Polish national art treasures from the Wawel royal castle in Cracow. He requested that arrangements be made to permit the entry, free of customs inspection, of these articles, as Polish state property. On July 16, 1940, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was informed by the assistant commissioner of customs that free entry of these items had been arranged at Halifax and Ottawa.
Subsequently, at the request of the Polish consul-general, the Department of Public Works provided storage space for the treasures in the records storage building at the central experimental farm. These facilities were granted to the Polish authorities on the clear understanding that the Canadian government assumed no responsibilty for the safekeeping of these articles. No inventory of the treasures was given to the Canadian government. From the time that the treasures were deposited the representatives in Canada of the Polish government had sole access to the room where the treasures were stored, and they alone were responsible for the safekeeping of this property.
In 1945. after the retreat of the German armies, a new government was established in Poland. This government was unconditionally recognized by the government of Canada on July 16. 1945, on which date recognition was
automatically withdrawn from the Polish government-in-exile which had its headquarters in London.
On May 16 and again on May 18, 1946, a representative of the legation of the newly recognized government of Poland called on the Department of External Affairs and stated that not all the Polish treasures were in the room which had been made available for the use of the Polish authorities at the central experimental farm but that parts had been dispersed to various places in Canada. This was the first indication to officials of the Canadian government that some of the treasures had been removed from the records storage building, presumably by the Polish officials originally in charge of these articles.
On June 21, 1946, the Polish legation in Ottawa informed the Department of External Affairs that, in the spring of 1945, a large part of the Polish art treasures which had been stored in the records storage building at the central experimental farm had been removed to certain places in Ottawa and in the country, and requesting the Department of External Affairs to protect these treasures.
The attitude of the Department of External Affairs was fully set forth in a reply sent to the Polish minister in Canada, on August 2,
1946.	It was pointed out that, while a place of storage had been provided for these treasures, the Canadian government had not accepted responsibility for their safekeeping, and that, from the original date of storage until May, 1945, officials of the government of Canada had had no access to them. The Polish minister was also advised that, after information had been received that some of the treasures had been removed, a new lock had been placed on the door of the storage room at the public records building where the treasures had been placed, and that since that time access to the room had been permitted to no one but Canadian officials. As a courtesy to the Polish legation in Canada, and without accepting responsibility in the matter, the Department of External Affairs had communicated with various companies and institutions where, according to an officer of the Polish legation, certain of the Polish art treasures had been stored. As a result of these inquiries the Bank of Montreal stated that it was holding in safekeeping two locked
Polish Art Treasures

steamer trunks which, it was understood, contained property of the Polish state. Other inquiries failed to reveal the location of other missing articles. In this note it was also suggested to the Polish minister that he should arrange as soon as possible to remove those art treasures still stored in the records storage building, experimental farm.
On November 12, 1946, the Polish minister called on the Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs and asked for the help of the Canadian government in locating the missing treasures. The Polish minister stated that he had been unable to obtain any information from the institutions in Canada to which the articles had been removed, concerning their then location. On this occasion it was again pointed out to the Polish minister that the only connection the Canadian government had had with the storage of the Polish art treasures was that the Department of Public Works had made a room available to the representative of the Polish government and had handed over to him the keys of that room. At no time prior to the arrival of the representatives of the new Polish government did the Canadian authorities have an inventory of the art treasures, and at no time had the Canadian government undertaken their safekeeping.
On November 13, 1946, the Polish minister, in a note to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, gave detailed lists of the treasures, part of which it was stated had disappeared from a monastery at Ste. Anne de Beaupre, and another part of which had disappeared from a convent in Ottawa. In the note the Polish minister again requested the assistance of the Canadian government in locating the missing treasures.
Following the receipt of this note, the Department of External Affairs made further inquiries in an attempt to learn where the missing treasures were located, but without success.
On December 16, 1946, a lawyer who had been consulted by persons having possession of the missing articles called on the Undersecretary of State for External Affairs. He suggested that an arrangement might be made by which the property in question could be restored to the Polish state by agreement at the end of a five year period. His suggestion was that in the meantime the treasures would be placed on public exhibition throughout Canada. He proposed also that as a gesture of good will between the people of Canada and the people of Poland the Canadian government might arrange with the Polish authorities for an exhibition of Canadian art in the cities of Poland during the period that the Polish treasures were on display in Canada.

speechtext:
You had better give his name.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Then I will. It was Mr. Leonard Brockington, who is a gentleman usually recognized as a lawyer of high standing.
It was further suggested that certain articles included in the collection of Polish treasures which it was claimed were the property of individuals, churches, and other institutions, should, at the end of the five year period, be returned to their beneficial owners. Officials of the Department of External Affairs stated that the department could not recognize any other than the present Polish government as entitled to property which had been brought here and entered as belonging to the Polish state, but nevertheless they undertook to explore with this lawyer the terms upon which agreement might be reached and the Polish legation in Ottawa was informed of this development. Eventually, after prolonged discussions concerning which the Polish legation was kept constantly informed, a proposal was submitted informally to the Polish authorities for their consideration. According to the terms of this proposal the Canadian government would have accepted custody of the art treasures for a period of five years, defraying during that time the costs of insurance, maintenance and transportation.
The Canadian authorities had no particular desire to accept custody of the treasures, nor to bear the expenses involved in holding them for a period of five years. They offered to do so merely because this appeared to be a necessary condition of securing an agreement whereby the treasures might be restored to the Polish government without further dispute. It was hoped that the government's willingness to accept this responsibility would be regarded by the Polish government as an evidence of the good intentions of the Canadian authorities and of their desire to assist in settling the matter.

Polish Art Treasures
The Polish government rejected this basis of settlement as, of course, it was fully entitled to do. No Canadian official at any time suggested that the Polish government should choose to settle this question by agreement if it would prefer to seek a solution otherwise. The charge d'affaires of the Polish legation subsequently addressed a further note to us on September 29, 1947. This note was accompanied by a statement in which the circumstances leading to the loss of the treasures were outlined and in which a formal request was made that legal proceedings be initiated to apprehend those responsible for the removal of the treasures. A request was also made for action by the police authorities to locate the objects themselves. The statement further requested that steps be taken to prevent the missing articles or any part of them from being removed from Canada.
I replied to his communication that, while the government of Canada had no responsibility for the safekeeping of these treasures, it had been decided, in order to assist the government of Poland in the recovery of the missing objects, and since the efforts to bring about the return of the treasures by agreement have not been successful, to request the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to undertake a search in an effort to ascertain the location of the missing articles.
As regards the request that legal proceedings be initiated against those in possession, or thought to be in possession, of the missing property, the Polish charge d'affaires was advised that the government of Poland was at perfect liberty to proceed itself in this matter through the Canadian courts. '
In the note to the Polish charge d'affaires attention was also drawn to the inaccurate statements concerning the treasures which had been appearing in the Polish press, some of which were attributed to officials of the foreign ministry. It was pointed out that the Department of External Affairs had been, glad to lend its assistance to the representative of Poland in Canada in order to secure the earliest possible return of the treasures to Poland. It was therefore regretted that these efforts had been incorrectly interpreted to the people of Poland and the hope was expressed that steps would be taken by the Polish government to correct misapprehensions which had arisen as a result of reports originating in Poland.
What was done afterwards appears from the following statement issued to the press last night by the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police:
On December 21, 1947, the Minister of External Affairs requested the Minister of Justice to
instruct the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to ascertain the then location of the missing Polish art treasures and further, if the missing articles were located, to endeavour to keep the same under surveillance until a decision could be reached as to what action might be taken by the Polish legation.
The Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was so instructed and in January, 1948, was in a position to report that a portion of the treasure consisting of 23 trunks and one box had been located stored in l'Hotel Dieu, Quebec City, a hospital and religious institution. The trunks and box had previously been stored in the Redemptorist monastery at Ste. Anne de Beaupre, Que.
When information was received by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that the articles had been removed to the Hotel Dieu, a competent and experienced non-commissioned officer, Corporal J. R. R. Oarriere, accompanied by another member1 of the police, Constable Houle, interviewed the Mother Superior in charge of the institution, stating that they had been requested to locate the missing Polish art treasures.
The Mother Superior on learning the purpose of the visit quite readily informed the members of the police that the treasures were still in the basement of the convent andi offered to show them to the members. The offer was accepted and the room containing the treasures was visited by the two members of the police, accompanied by the Mother 'Superior and her assistant.
It was the Mother 'Superior who directed the police through the cloister, although in fact the police offered to proceed' to the basement by an outside entrance.
The purpose of the interview was to seek information and the R.C.M.P. made no demand to enter, much less was there any suggestion that they had a right 'to search. They were received most courteously by the Mother Superior.
At a later date Inspector Rene J. Belec again interviewed the Mother Superior and was received in a most co-operative and understanding manner.
The police were fully aware that there was a dispute as to the rightful ownership or possession of the articles and the Commissioner of the police had specifically instructed that they should be treated as missing property and that no demand could be made to produce the property nor if located should any seizure action be taken.
As to the statement to which I referred yesterday as having been handed to me just before I came into the house and as being so extraordinary in its terms and inaccurate in its assertions that I wished to ascertain whether or not it really had been made before dealing with it, I have now found that it was made and I must repeat that it contains many assertions which are not true. Thus in the first paragraph it is said that a short while ago members of the federal police without search warrants and in an illegal manner, forced their entrance not only into the convent of the Sisters of the Hotel Dieu but also into their cloister.

This is an untrue statement and hon. members will have seen in this morning's papers that the Reverend Mother Superior of the convent has given it a dignified but no less unqualified denial. I think her statement should also be made a part of their record. As reported in the press, it is as follows:
A few months ago we were asked to receive from a very respectable gentleman of Polish nationality and to safeguard parcels containing, we were then told, 'articles of 'art and value.
In ordler to oblige we accepted the task and the packages were brought here. Things remained: thus for a while and we took all care possible of the deposit in- our custody to ensure their safety.
During the month of February another gentleman, also of Polish nationality, under' the title of "agent" for the Polish republic, claimed that said parcels should be entrusted to him.
Informed of this task, the first person, who had put the deposit in our charge, strictly forbade ua to give the said parcels away; he strengthened! his order by reminding us that according to law we were not allowed to remit the deposit in question'-a deposit in trust-to anyone but himself, ,and ordered the removal of the parcels to the provincial museum.
We then addressed ourselves to the Prime Minister1 of the province of Quebec, who consented to the transportation- of the aforementioned 'articles to the museum. We believed the museum a safe place for the valuables.
We are willing to admit that our religious community had no reasons at all to permit a trial between the two gentlemen in question to implicate us. The provincial government, on its part, had told us of its intention to conform itself to the tribunal's decision.
We wiant it noted and understood' that there was never a "saisie" (seizure) in our monastery by the provincial government, and that the deposit was never at any time under the protection of the R.C.M.P.
We accepted the deposit in good faith and we returned it according to instructions received from the person v-ho had entrusted the valuables to our care in the first place.
That is the end of the statement which I was very happy to read this morning in the newspapers and about which I can assure the house I had no previous intimation. The suggestion in Mr. Duplessis' statement that there was a violation of the cloister is quite ridiculous. His statement further says:
We are much grieved that the federal authorities of our country, particularly the ministers representing the province of Quebec in. the country's government, made themselves the collaborators of Stalin and his Polish government to the point that they ordered their police to ignore the laws -and to violate the cloister of that noble order.
When one notes that this clumsy but deliberate attempt to smear the ministers representing the province of Quebec in the country's government, and remembers that he is preparing for a provincial election, one can only

deplore that Mr. Duplessis should expect such tactics to win for him from well informed sources anything but contempt.

Mr. ST. LAURENT: I am not sure that I understand fully the purport of the hon. member's interjection, but as I understand it, I thank him for it. I am glad to hear that he agrees that not much else but what I have said could be expected from such a course.

What I was saying was that we also do not like these accusations when they come to us unduly from other sources.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The statement goes on to say that the government of the province of Quebec "has seized and impounded these treasures." This is what the federal government had been asked to do but had refused to do, informing those who made the request that in this country the executive government did not seize and impound objects to which there were disputing claimants; that all we could do would be to ascertain if possible where the objects were and the disputing claimants would then have to resort to the courts for an adjudication upon their rights if they saw fit to do so.
Now whatever may be the views of individuals with respect to the present government of Poland, the fact is that it is and it has been for over two years the legal government of that country recognized as such by all civilized nations, and the federal authorities have never felt and do not feel that they are acting as "accomplices" of that government in saying to it, as they would say to the government of any other sovereign state, that it is free to resort to the courts of Canada to assert and enforce any rights it may have as such to .property actually situate in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the house will regret that there has been any loss of articles from the place of storage provided by this government for treasures from another country. We also regret it if there has been any misunderstanding thus created between these two nations through this loss or the movement of these articles. I wish to ask only one question. It arises from three statements of fact which I put down as the minister spoke.
The first was that the government accepted or allowed to be stored at the experimental farm about the year 1940 these Polish treasures. The second was, as we are all aware, that in

Polish Art Treasures
1945 a new government assumed power in Poland, which new government was recognized by this government as the legitimate government of Poland at that time. The third fact was that in 1946 this government was advised that certain of these articles had disappeared from the place of storage at the experimental farm.
So far as I am concerned the question I intend to ask is the only pertinent one. If through any action on our part, even though we took no responsibility for these treasures, if through any sin of omission or commission some of these articles have been lost, we regret it and perhaps deserve some censure. My question is this: Were any special steps taken after 1940 to protect the treasures stored at the experimental farm? Particularly after the change in government in Poland in 1945 were any special steps taken to see that they did not disappear?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No other steps were taken than those I have indicated in the statement I made to the house.

Perhaps I had better answer that question. The situation with respect to ceilings on meat, including beef, is this. The government announced late in January, I think, that it intended to reimpose ceilings on meat and

on butter; and it was pointed out at that time that the imposition of retail ceilings on meat involved quite a technical operation in working out what those ceilings should be with respect to, I am told, nearly 200 items. When we adjourned I had mentioned the need in Canada of a real immigration policy, and had said that I thought this should be brought about because of the help that was needed in agriculture. In view of the fact that it is our basic industry I believe everything should be done to provide labour for the farms. We seldom stop to consider that every hon. member, and indeed every individual in the world, depends on the basic industry of agriculture for his very existence; yet in many places agriculture is regarded more or less as a necessary evil. Many people go into the grocery stores and butcher shops and think-

I should like to make a suggestion, Mr. Speaker. I notice that when questions on the orders of the day have been concluded there is a great exodus from the house, and a lot of talk is carried on. I am not speaking on behalf of myself alone, but on behalf of all hon. members. When the order of the day is proceeded with and a member rises to speak, it is not fair to have to compete against so much confusion, but that is what happens every day when an hon. member rises to speak. So far as I am concerned what
I have to say may not be very interesting, but I think any hon. member who rises to address the house should be extended some courtesy and consideration.
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that in many circles agriculture is looked upon as a necessary evil; that many of the people who go into the grocery and butcher shops think that the products there grow on the shelves of the shops. Large amounts of money are being spent in research in order that farming may be carried on more scientifically, and yet at the same time no encouragement is being given to the young people of Canada to stay on the farm. It is the young people who will put these new methods into operation, and not the older farmers of today.
It has also been said that farmers will not or do not pay good wages. I maintain, sir, that the farmers of this country will pay good wages for good help if they are given good prices for their products.
I should like to refer to a few matters particularly affecting my own constituency. The apple industry is one of the large industries in the county I have the honour to represent. An outline of it might be given from a letter which I received from some of the growers. It reads as follows:
The first commercial orchards in, Northumberland and Durham were started -around 1885. Since that time this district has forged steadily ahead until now it is well over a million-dollar business with a production of three-quarters of *a million bushels annually. In keeping with consumer preference the varieties have changed from- chiefly Ben Davis and Spy until now McIntosh, iSpy and Delicious make up the major portion of the production.
A new trend) in marketing is developing. The more progressive commercial growers now realize they must get their apples to the consumer in a more direct fashion and with less overhead than has been the practice in the last few years. This trend which has been started now will have a very beneficial effect both on the grading and the consumer acceptance of apples from this district.
That is to say, our growers realize that they will have to present their apples to the consumer in a much better condition than they have in the past. Canadian Canners have a factory in my constituency. Realizing this year that there was a market for such products as apple juice and apple sauce, they established a line, using much of the equipment that they had put together for canning peas and various other vegetables. The result was they finally installed a line by which they processed apple juice and other products of the apple. For that purpose the firm bought 90,000 barrels of apples and processed them. This naturally took off the market poorer grades of apples

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the house for long, but there are some observations I should like to make. First may I express a word of congratulation to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Perhaps I may be pardoned if I make special reference to .the young member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), who seconded the address. He spent many of his younger days in my home town of Antigonish, and naturally I have followed his career with interest.
For the most part my remarks this afternoon will deal with matters that affect the maritime provinces, and perhaps more particularly the constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough, which I have the honour to represent. This constituency has varied interests, with an extensive shoreline along the rock-bound coast bordering the Atlantic ocean from the Halifax county line to the strait of Canso, thence along this strait to St. George's bay and thence to Northumberland strait and the Pictou county line. It is but natural, therefore, that fishing should play a prominent part in the lives of many of my constituents.
At this point I should like to make some reference to the recent appointment of the new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacKinnon). I am sure he will give this department the same careful attention that was so characteristic of his efforts on behalf of Canada when he was Minister of Trade and Commerce. If the Department of Fisheries develops under his able administration as his former department did during his tenure of office, I look forward to great strides being made by the fisheries of Canada.
But our fishing industry cannot develop single-handed, without more modern fishing methods. Only those who go down to the sea in ships know the rigours of the industry and the hardships endured by our seafaring men. One of the first suggestions I would like to make to the government is that improved aids to navigation should be provided as quickly as possible. By this I mean increased buoy service and the installation of power fog alarms which can be heard for some distance, rather than the numerous hand-operated fog alarms now in use that can be heard only a short distance away. Then, too.
The Address-Mr. Kirk

I think better protection can and should be given our fishermen in the matter of what I shall call a mother ship. This is something I have been advocating for a good many years with the various ministers of fisheries. It is true that during the war the supplying of many needs of the fishermen had to be deferred, but there is not the same excuse for not taking action now. This need is recognized by the Department of Fisheries; for I have a letter written only a year ago by the then minister in which he advised me that it was appreciated by the department that our patrol service needs to be built up, but as far as I can find out no progress in this direction has been made.
In connection with the suggestion of a mother ship, it seems to me that a proper coastguard marine service to a large extent would 'take care of the hazards with which the fishermen are faced every day they pursue their activities. I was sorry to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) say a few days ago that the cost of a coastguard marine would be prohibitive. I wonder if this statement was made after the situation had been thoroughly canvassed. It is reported that more than a year ago the R.C.M.P. were studying the possibility of establishing a new coastguard, not only for the east and west coasts but also for the great lakes, which would incorporate in one service the various seagoing activities of the government, dealing with customs, immigration, hydrographic sendee, fisheries patrol, transport inspection, air-sea rescue, and so on. As it is now we have these government marine services operating under various controls but unable to function in connection with rescue service with the efficiency that a well organized coastguard service could effect. I would say to the minister that his statement will not meet with much if any approval on the part of anyone in Canada. I believe those living inland, making their livelihood by other means than the sea, are genuinely interested in the welfare of our seamen; but particularly will his statement be met with something bordering on hostility by the families of those living by the sea and making their living on the sea. I suggest that the minister or the government have a thorough investigation made into the possibility of combining the services I have mentioned into one efficient organization. This combined service ordinarily could carry out the usual duties; but in emergency cases, operating under the direction of one authority, the most easily accessible rescue crew could be instructed to proceed to the assistance of those reported to be in danger.

I now turn to a subject which I think should be dealt with by the Minister of Fisheries, that is the matter of assisting groups of fishermen who have organized themselves into co-operatives which buy, process and sell fish, by giving them financial assistance in the matter of equipping their plants with mechanical freezers, cold storage plants and mechanical fish driers. The same assistance could well be given to other fish buyers who are not financially able to provide the modem equipment which is needed if we are to keep abreast of the times and provide the quality of fish demanded by the consumer.
While speaking on behalf of our fishermen I naturally think of the benefits the Department. of Public Works can render these people. I am speaking, of course, of wharves, breakwaters and dredging that should and must be done if our fishermen are to continue to pursue their calling. In all fairness I think I should say the department has been pretty fair to our fishermen in the matter of keeping in repair the structures built in days gone by. But I do not think I will be unfair if I go so far as to say that in the matter of new wharves and breakwaters which are sorely needed along the coastline the department has been holding back too long. In the matter of dredging I can only endorse, in effect, what I have said on the floor of this chamber before, and on many occasions by personal conversation and by letter to the minister. The Department of Public Works either owns too few dredges or too many. I say this because at the present time private enterprise concerns are short of dredges. One of the reasons may be that dredging has to some extent been unprofitable, inasmuch as private enterprise had to compete with the Department of Public Works estimates or costs, which costs I am satisfied were not their actual dredging costs, inasmuch as many overhead charges did not enter into the cost of operation.
About a year ago I suggested to the minister, when his estimates were before the committee, that the department get busy and build dredges that would be capable of doing a certain type of dredging required along the shores of the maritime provinces. The minister, if I remember correctly, intimated that was the intention of the government. To date, however, as far as I can find out, there have been no dredges of this type built, nor indeed are there any being built. All this is a delay which should not occur, and postpones the time when the necessary dredging will be accomplished. I urge upon the minister that he see to it that orders are placed as quickly

The Address-Mr. Kirk
as possible for a number of dredges sufficient to do the required dredging within a reasonable period of time.
Perhaps the minister will feel like telling the house that steel is in short supply, and that until such time as steel is more readily available the construction of these dredges will have to be deferred. To this I would say- yes, steel may be in short supply, but I think that' which is available should be directed into channels where it can be made best use of. I am thinking now of steel used in the construction of theatres, bowling alleys and other construction work which is not necessary to the economy of the country. What I have said of steel applies also to wood, which has been in short supply. I am thinking now of timber needed in the construction of the wharves and breakwaters that I have been talking about.
Having dealt briefly with the problems of the fisheries, I want to discuss some of the problems of our farmers. In the more sheltered portions of the two counties of Antigonish and Guysborough, the uplands and meadows provide very fertile soil for the pursuits of agriculture, and many of our people live comfortably, though not extravagantly, on the mixed farming which is there carried on with a measure of success.
Last week the members from Nova Scotia had a call from the Hon. A. W. Mackenzie, minister of agriculture for Nova Scotia, who with his deputy minister discussed with us the proposals for reclamation of marshlands in Nova Scotia, freshwater soil erosion, rehabilitation of the apple industry, and feed grain freight assistance. To Canada's Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) I can say that the members from Nova Scotia strongly recommend the acceptance and carrying out of the proposals made by our provincial minister of agriculture. The proposals are perhaps the most comprehensive ever placed before the government for consideration by representa-tivs of maritime interests. We feel we are not asking for anything but what is needed, and can be justified, and is within our rights.
At this time the most urgent information required by our farmers is to know whether or not the feed grain freight assistance is to be continued beyond July next so that they can make their plans accordingly. This uncertainty must be eliminated, and very soon. Otherwise I fear many of our farmers will make plans that will be detrimental not only to themselves but to the country as a whole, to the extent that they supply our own food requirements, plus a surplus for export, either to other provinces in the dominion, to the United States, or overseas.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, I have been dealing with two of our primary industries, agriculture and fisheries. At this point, I should like to pay tribute to the work being done by the university of St. Francis Xavier, situated in my home town of Antigonish. Through its extension department, its adult study clubs and its short courses, this university has done much to assist our farmers and fishermen to improve their methods of production and their standards of living
The university has also been a pioneer in the promoting of the Rochdale principles of cooperation; and indeed its fame in this respect has spread far and wide, as witness the students from all parts of the world who crowd its halls. From South America, from the United States, from Newfoundland, the West Indies and the British isles, even from far-off China, have come those who are anxious to learn the principles of co-operation as taught at St. Francis Xavier, in order that they may carry to their own lands this program of adult education and economic co-operation.
As one result of the work being done by the Antigonish movement, many co-operative industries have come into being among the fishermen and farmers of our maritime provinces. These industries, owned by the "little people" themselves, have steadily progressed.
This brings me along, Mr. Speaker, to a subject which is uppermost in the minds of our co-operatives today, that of taxation. The cooperatives object to the present income tax act as applied to them. I do not think there is anything further that I can add to the arguments used last year when this matter was discussed in the budget debate. It is my opinion however that these co-operatives should be given every assistance possible by governments, both local and federal; and I would suggest to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that, before bringing down the budget this year, he consider again very carefully this matter of co-operative taxation. He will, I believe, find reason to exempt from taxation bona fide co-operative enterprises which are profit-sharing rather than profit-making.
The counties of Antigonish and Guysborough also contain fine stretches of timber, both hard and soft wood; but the lumber industry has been greatly handicapped by lack of suitable means of transportation.
As I have pointed out on various occasions, the whole county of Guysborough is practically without any railroad. This Guysborough railway has been used, by both old-line parties, as a political football ever since confederation. True, no government is bound by anything a candidate may say at election time or between
The Address-Mr. Kirk

elections; but this case is somewhat different, for the Liberal government has in effect promised the people of Guysborough a railway, inasmuch as a contract was let and construction work begun in 1029. Unfortunately before the contract was completed there was a change of government and the new Conservative administration under the late Right Hon. R. B. Bennett cancelled the contract, and from that day to this, nothing further has been done about it.
Naturally, during the war years, the good people of Guysborough county were satisfied to wait, believing that every available dollar should be expended in fighting the enemy. But now that the war is over, and we have gone through the transition period from war to peace, they do expect this government to fulfil the promise made to them, as I have said, away back in 1929.
I was pleased to learn that a three-man board of engineers will shortly begin study on the possibilities of improving transportation facilities across the strait of Canso. If the industries of Cape Breton are to develop, a more modem transportation system is essential. If a bridge or causeway in structurally possible, I submit that the government should proceed with the building of this link just as quickly as possible. The construction of a bridge or causeway will benefit not only the people living on the island of Cape Breton, but those in the rest of the province of Nova Scotia and other parts of Canada as well.
I would not wish to complete my remarks today without saying something in support of increases in old age pensions, blind pensions and pensions for disabled veterans. I will go so far as to say that if the revenue of the country will not provide for these increases in pensions or, if you will, bonuses scaled to meet the cost of living as it rises and falls, then in my opinion there should be no reduction in income taxes until these groups of people have been granted such increases as I have indicated.
From time to time we hear some people give their views on subsidies, some in favour, some opposed. My opinion is something like this. Theoretically, there should be no subsidies, but factually there are times when they are justified and there is no dollar sign that can determine this. The need is and should be the determining factor. The direct or indirect benefits, as I said before, cannot be computed in dollars and cents, but no doubt play a commensurate part in the country's economy. When subsidies are asked for I suggest that the government give very careful thought to the over-all benefits, before

saying either yes or no, but particularly before saying no without most careful consideration.
In conclusion, I wish to say through you, sir, to the government of the day, in fact to any government at any time in charge of Canadian affairs, that they will have to give, not only consideration but favourable consideration supported by deeds and not words, to the various phases of our maritime economy, some of which I have already enumerated.
I know, Mr. Speaker, it is probably much easier, for some of us at any rate, to be nasty than to be nice, and speaking for myself I do not want to appear nasty when I use the word "warn". But I do wish to warn the government that the people in the maritimes who have given this country such loyal support in any and all endeavours for the general good and welfare of Canada expect that the Liberal government, which has done more for Canada under the leadership of our present Prime Minister than any other government has done since confederation-I repeat, those in the maritimes expect that this government will see to it that they are given equal opportunities with those residing in other parts of this great dominion. Failing this, I fear we will not continue to enjoy the unity which our Prime Minister has always stressed and which is so desirable and so necessary if Canada is to continue to progress.
Mr. DOUGLAS G. ROSS (St. Paul's): Mr. Speaker, I wish to compliment the last speaker and, as you will find out in the latter part of my remarks, I have particular reasons for doing so. I do not agree with everything he said. He suggested that the Liberal government have done more for Canada than any other government in history. Of course I do not agree with that because I think they have done more harm than any other government, and the people of Canada realize that at the present time.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Stephenson) upon the remarks he made at the conclusion of his speech when he suggested that something should be done about communists. In Toronto there are something like 30,000 known communists. When a known communist such as Smith who was educated at the school of Stalin in Moscow can command 47,000 votes when running for controller it seems to me it is about time to take cognizance of the danger of communism in this country.
I do not intend to detain the house long on this occasion. As a matter of fact, I had not intended to speak, but there is one thing which I think every hon. member has had

The Address-Mr. D. G. Ross
thrown at him in the last little while, something which affects every member of the House of Commons, and I did not think I should let this opportunity go by without saying a few words about it. I refer to the reading of speeches in the house. The prohibition in this regard is contained in standing order 41, citation 293. I shall have more to say about this later on.
Debate on the address gives hon. members an opportunity to state the grievances of their constituents. All the arguments are heard by hon. members and at the conclusion of the debate a vote is taken. The government stands or falls by the result of that vote,. In other words, it is a vote of confidence in the government. I am certainly' not going to vote for this government.
This debate gives hon. members an opportunity to tell of the advantages of their constituencies and to tell of the accomplishments of their constituents. I do not need to do that because my riding is the most important riding in Canada. I do not intend to give my reasons for saying that at the present time; I do not need to discuss it because everybody knows that it is. The constituents in my riding certainly have grievances and I intend to mention a few as I go along. The constituents in other parts of Canada also have grievances. Under this government there are plenty of grievances, and I shall mention just a few.
First of all, there is the inadequacy of veterans' pensions. Even the new scale does not provide the standard of living which a veteran should have. There is also the inadequacy of widows' pensions and the inadequacy of the civil service superannuation. Those people paid into the superannuation fund when a dollar bought a dollar's worth of goods, but now when they are getting their pension the same dollar buys only about fifty cents worth of goods. There is also the question of the lack of housing accommodation and the scarcity of shared accommodation.
There is the iniquitous tax of two cents on pop and chocolate bars for children, and there is also the iniquitous luxury tax on many necessities of life. As an example, take a watch selling for 82.69, the kind of watch a boy wants, a utility watch for a man. The tax on that watch is 25 per cent, or sixty-seven cents. That is only one instance in hundreds of cases.
Everybody' is affected by the lack of vision on the part of this government in the development of our natural resources. The government have shown great tardiness in respect to its immigration policy and in respect to the *obstructions which were placed in the way of the province of Ontario when they wanted to 5849-1194
bring in immigrants to this province. Then there is the stubbornness and stupidity on the part of the government in the handling of the United States dollar shortage. It is hard to believe that there could be anything more stupid or lacking in foresight than that. There are many more grievances which I could mention and which I shall have an opportunity of speaking about at some future time.
I come now to a matter which affects every every member of the House of Commons, the reading of speeches. I know there are varied opinions with regard to this. I do not wish to criticize any member for reading his speech or delivering it otherwise just as he likes. The rule against reading speeches originated in the distant past when some members perhaps did not have the educational advantages which the present membership of the house has, and sometimes they would get someone outside the house to put down their thoughts on paper for delivery in the house. Some perhaps did not have their own thoughts but somebody else's put down on paper for them to read, and so the rule against reading speeches was made. But today it is a relic of the dark ages. I doubt if any member today gets an outsider to write his speech for him. It is not necessary because, despite what might be said in some quarters, I have a very high opinion of the intellectual ability of the members of the House of Commons.
Today if an objection is made to a member reading his speech, Your Honour points to the rule which says he must not read his speech. Often a member reading his speech will be interrupted, as was the case the other day when one of our French-speaking members attempted to read his speech in English. I think he should have been allowed to do so without interruption, but he was interrupted and there was a delay in consequence. Finally he bow'ed to Your Honour's ruling and said that he would stick closely to his notes.
I suggest that a member who reads his speech in the House of Commons should not be interrupted. I do not like reading my speeches, but when you want to be careful in what you say you have to stick closely to your notes. Many speeches delivered in the House of Commons have been read; there is no doubt about that, and there is an unfairness about the thing because one member reading his speech will be interrupted and attention called to the rule, while another is allowed to go on reading without any interruptions. I think a change should be made in this rule. If the speeches generally were more carefully prepared and read they could be made much shorter and more concise. All
The Address-Mr. D. G. Ross

of us are not so gifted in oratory that we can say briefly what we want to say in clear and concise language. There is a certain amount of fumbling and stumbling and repetition. I have heard long speeches made in this house containing much repetition and perhaps some of the main points the speaker intended to make were overlooked.
I do not think all' prepared speeches which are read in the house are mechanical or lifeless. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) rose in his place this afternoon and said that he was making a statement, but he was really reading a statement. It is certainly true that some speeches which are read are lifeless. On the other hand, I have heard many able speeches read in the house.

No one would say that the great speeches of Mr. Churchill are lifeless or mechanical or wooden; yet nearly all his major speeches were read from prepared manuscript, and the same was true of Mr. Roosevelt. Many ministers of the crown read their speeches in this house; we all know that. Sometimes they are called statements, but they are speeches just the same. If we are to have one rule in this house for ministers and another rule for the other members it is time we got rid of the rule. I feel strongly about this. In past times the rule may have been wise, but I doubt if it serves any useful purpose today. The purpose for which it was made has gone. A farce is made of the rule today.
I have heard some very good speeches read in this house, as, for example, that of the hon. gentleman who preceded me. His speech was a very thoughtful one and a compliment to the membership of this house.
With all due deference, Mr. Speaker, I have a few constructive suggestions to make on this subject, one of which I have made before.
First, I would say that if a member so desires he should be allowed to hand in any written, non-controversial speech, and if, upon examination, it is found to be such, let it be

printed in an appendix to Hansard. That would take care of members who wish to extol the advantages of their constituencies.
Second, if a member desires to read his speech he should so announce to the house, and be limited to a shorter time for its delivery, say thirty minutes. I think that would make for speeches of shorter duration, or else.
Third, the rule ought to be rescinded or enforced. It is not being enforced at this time; therefore it is a farce. I am sure some change is necessary to prevent delays and to ensure respect for this house. I am not speaking on behalf of hon. members alone;
I am speaking on behalf of the general public of the country. I think the public would be far better served if hon. members were allowed to have their speeches prepared in typewritten form, everything put in a concise form, and then to deliver them to the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for quite some time our people have been worried, and rightly, over the economic conditions of our country and the trend of our public policies.
They are worried, notably, over the gradual and steady rise in the cost of living ever since the war ended and which has now reached a point where many families are deprived of the necessaries of life in a country where production is abundant, while we are selling a large part of that production to strangers at ridioulously low prices or giving it to them outright. In other words they are worried over this poverty in the midst of plenty. They are further disturbed by the shortage of housing and the insanitary condition of houses where large families are being crowded, in a country producing almost twice its normal timber requirements.
They view with apprehension the unprecedented extravagance with strangers while they themselves are subjected to an austerity program and crushed under a burden of taxes causing special hardships to large families.
Another reason for concern is our financial situation which causes us to borrow from our neighbours while lending to others without any hope of reimbursement.
In spite of the many warnings by competent authorities, that a country cannot forever at the same time buy cash and sell on credit or simply give away its goods overseas, our government has ignored this simple truth and maintained its policy of lavish gifts to foreigners and of hardship for its own people until the time came when something had to

___________The Address-Mr. M. Raymond
be done and our whole economic structure was threatened with collapse. Such are the conditions facing us at the beginning of 1948.
The measures proposed by the government to restore the equilibrium of our economy are not such as to allay our fears. An investigation committee cannot stop the increasing cost of living; the government should have used every available means to prevent that increase. On the other hand, we cannot hope to lower the cost of living by restricting imports of American goods, as this will only create a greater scarcity of much needed consumer goods. On the contrary, scarcity of goods will cause prices to rise.
A 25 per cent excise tax on consumer goods is not the proper way of lowering the cost of living.
It is not sufficient to state in the speech from the throne that "Canada has continued to enjoy general prosperity" and to boast that our help to devastated countries has been unequalled by other nations. Such statements cannot make us forget that in Montreal, for instance, thousands are living in squalor and *without proper shelter, and do not relieve the government of responsibility in the matter.
Misery and austerity in a land of prosperity and plenty are dangerous and paradoxical contradictions that can only beget communism.
Any evil must be quelled at its source. What is the basic reason for our economic muddle? It can be summed up in a single sentence:	All our policies, internal as well
as external, hinge on favouring British interests at the expense of Canada.
To anyone who cares to review the government's actions during and since the war, it is clear that the main concern of this administration has been to serve the empire first without any regard for Canadian needs or interests. Our economic, commercial, financial, domestic, and immigration policies, as well as our policy of assistance to war-ravaged countries all are subservient to British interests.
While the war lasted, the slogan we went by was:	"To the last man and to the last
cent for the protection of British possessions". Since the end of the war, our new motto has been : "To the last cent so that Great Britain
may rebuild her economic might and recover her world market at our expense."
When we declared war in 1939 it was not, as a lying propaganda would have us believe, to defend Canada, or civilization, or the freedom of smaller nations, or democracy, or the respect of borders and treaties, but only because England had gone to war to protect her world supremacy, her trade, her various interests on every continent.
Can we protect civilization by means of an alliance with the most barbarous people that ever lived, the Russian people? Can we maintain fredom by uniting with the country now crushing surrounding small nations underfoot? Can we uphold democracy by uniting with the greatest of all dictators? Can we defend treaties with a country that has broken all treaties? Can we protect the territorial integrity of small nations with a large country annexing all neighbouring small nations?
No. Let us not fool the people any longer.
To be brief, I shall only mention a few official statements quite significant as far as the tendencies of our foreign policy under the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) are concerned.
When England declared war on Germany, on September 3, 1939, prime minister Neville Chamberlain indicated that this action had been taken to honour a signature to a treaty, ensuring the territorial integrity of Poland.
Mr. Churchill, addressing himself to this house on December 30, 1941, stated:
We plunged into this war all unprepared, because we had pledged omr w-ord to stand by the side of Poland which Hitler bad feloniously invaded.
Such was the reason given by England to their entry into the war with Germany. There was no mention of civilization, of Christian ideals, et cetera.
But Canada, who had no obligations towards Poland, could make no such claim. We learned later, in 1944, from the Prime Minister himself, that despite many claims to the contrary made in this house, and without the knowledge of parliament, he had committed this country to participating alongside Great Britain in a war against Germany, should the occasion arise. That was as early as 1937, at the time of the Imperial Conference. (See Hansard for 1944, page 6268).

The Address-Mr. M. Raymond
More than that, to show his devotion to the empire at the expense of Canada, the Prime Minister declared at a luncheon in Prince Albert on July 7, 1941, that at the time of the Munich conference in 1938, though the country was divided on the question of Canada's participation, he would have favoured the latter. Here is what he said:
(Text):
If wair had come at the time of the Munich conference, the country would' have divided on the question of Canada's participation.
I am sure even my own cabinet would have been divided. But had war come my advice to the government would have been what it was a year later when war came-to stand at the side of Britain.
(Translation):
Yet, in 1938, Mr. Chamberlain found that there was no point in fighting Germany over the claims of the Sudeten Germans of Czechoslovakia, which he believed well-founded. Sir John Simon even added:
Munich ensured the return to the Reich of a region which should never have been incorporated into Czechoslovak territory. In fact, we have, by our action in this matter, corrected one of the errors of the peace treaty.
Nevertheless, the Prime Minister was ready to launch Canada into war, had England entered an armed conflict. It was the carrying out of the imperialistic policy he expounded in the house on January 16, 1939. "When England is at war, we are at war,'' a slogan which Mr. Churchill took up once again in the British house on April 21, 1914, when he said that in 1939 the great principle whereby "When the king declares war, the empire is at war" had been upheld.
Our stand is determined according to the interests not of Canada but of the empire.
After war had been declared, we put forth a war effort proportionately greater than that of any other country. Yet, we did not have like Britain possessions to protect in Europe, in Asia or in Africa.
We went even further. We financed Great Britain which, however, owned and still owns investments in many parts of the world, and even in Canada.
Here is how Mr. Churchill acknowledged our contribution to the imperial effort, as he said, since it was the empire's war.
On December 30, 1941, speaking in this house, he said:
The contribution of Canada to the imperial war effort, im troops, in ships, in aircraft, in

food and in finance has been magnificent . . . The Canadian government has imposed no limitation upon the use of the Canadian army whether upon thq continent of Europe or elsewhere.
After this we are still expected to believe that when we went to Hong Kong, for instance, we fought for the defence of Canada.
But all this was not enough to satisfy our leaders' imperialistic fever. So we set out making first outright gifts then gifts disguised under various forms.
Gifts of money, gifts disguised under the form of mutual aid, cancellation of debt, subsidies on our export products, loans without interest and security, loss on the sale of our products at a price below world prices, etc., all of which adds up to a total which may reach seven or eight billions of dollars and which the Canadian people will have to pay in taxes.
The Canadian people are being bled white to allow England to restore her economy and resume her pre-war trade, at the risk of ruining this country.
Our policy is essentially imperialistic and anti-Canadian; our present diflfiieulties are the consequence of it all.
Why are we short of American dollars? First of all, because we have made loans beyond our means; then because it is forbidden to export to the United States certain farm products and other commodities, such as beef, that we could sell at quite profitable prices instead of giving them or selling them on credit and at lower prices to Great Britain.
The cost of living has greatly increased because we export most of our foodstuffs to Great Britain at a lower price than that paid by Canadian consumers.
As goods become scarcer here, prices rise. Since the end of the war, the cost of living has climbed steeply in Canada while it has remained practically unchanged in England.
Since it is now forbidden to import various consumer goods from the United States, there is a still greater scarcity of available commodities; further, the 25 per cent excise tax collected on a large number of products raises the cost of living. Such provisions, however, are in the interest of the British, as was explained by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and this seems to be the main consideration the present government keeps in mind.

The Address-Mr. M. Raymond
United Kingdom consumers are better off than Canadian consumers since they pay less for our products.
Government subsidies on commodities sold in Great Britain have been maintained and in some cases increased, while those that were paid on goods consumed in Canada were removed.
In 1946, for instance, we did away with the subsidy on liquid milk, step that raised the price of milk to the local consumer, but at the same time, we increased the subsidy on the milk required for our cheese production which is almost entirely sold to England. Who pays those subsidies? The Canadian taxpayer. Canadian consumers are taxed to help foreign consumers. But in order to make gifts of billions of dollars to Great Britain, we must have large revenues.
There is a housing shortage. In Montreal alone, 70,000 more houses would be needed and the speech from the throne refers to a lack of building materials. Why, for instance, this shortage of lumber? Too much of it has been shipped to England.
It is all very well to ship building materials to other nations that they may provide shelters for their people, but it is better still to provide homes for Canadians who are without them. There are people in Canada who are dying from the cold.
According to Le Canada of February 16, a citizen of the British Isles, who came to settle in this country, went back to England and stated on his return that the housing problem is more acute in Canada than in Great Britain. While duty bids us be charitable to others, we have, towards our fellow citizens, not only duties of charity but specific obligations.
There is no hesitation in taxing our people for the benefit of other countries but the government becomes stingy when it comes to provide services for our own nation.
Thus as a measure of economy-I see the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) is in his seat-rural postal service was abolished in certain districts because it cost too much.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Nowhere has it been abolished.

speechtext:
It has been claimed that the tenderers were asking too much. The hon. Postmaster General knows about it, for I called certain cases to his attention.
When the state lends to Canadian farmers, it asks an interest of 4) to 5 per cent, depending on the type of loan, but to the British, it lends without interest when it does not give.
One who serves the empire has more rights than one who serves his country. Thus a man who answered the call for military service in Canada does not have the same privileges as the man who served overseas. Why such discrimination? Why should it be more praiseworthy to defend a foreign country than one's own? This proves that our policy is fully and firstly at the empire's service. Canada comes next.
To justify our excessive lavishness towards the United Kingdom the government has heaped fallacy upon fallacy.
Some contended that the money loaned to Great Britain without interest and probably without security was good business and constituted a sort of insurance against unemployment. Knowing the facts, I have never been able to understand that argument.
1.	It is the only country to which we loaned money without interest. We did so in order to allow her to purchase from us at a price lower than the world price-and at a time when we had to do with rationing-foodstuffs and raw materials which we could have sold anytime and anywhere at a much higher price, because those commodities were much in demand.
2.	We will not find employment for our city workers by selling raw materials which will be transformed into manufactured products and compete with our own goods.
3.	In addition, those sales do not benefit us, since we are being paid with our own money, while we could sell to other countries for cash.
Others have said that our gesture was bound to ensure a future market for our products if and when the general demand decreases.
Facts have proven the fallacy of that argument. First, Great Britain will not buy our manufactured products because she herself depends on the export of her own manufactured goods.
As to buying our natural products and our raw materials, we are aware of the trade agreements she has made with several countries, including Russia, Poland, Denmark, Australia, Argentina and others. She buys raw materials which she processes for export. It is her right, which nobody can deny her. She tries to secure the best bargain. Hers is a truly national policy.
Thanks to our gifts and interest free loans, she is getting back on her feet and is out to

The Address-Mr. M. Raymond
win over various markets while stepping up the production of wheat and other foodstuffs.
Here is what we are told in a release handed out in December, 1947, by the United Kingdom Information Service:
(Text):
Before the war, Britain produced only one-third of its food . . . and today one-half of Britain's food is produced at home. The target is 'to raise this proportion to sixty per cent... Wheat output was more than doubled . . . British agriculture is to increase output by $400,000,000 or twenty per cent during the next five years.
(Translation):
Far from securing a future market for us, our making interest free and no doubt irrecoverable loans to England in order to sell her our goods at less than world prices, while we were making interest bearing loans to countries like China, Holland, France, Belgium and Norway who pay us world prices, will probably cause us to lose our markets in these countries and elsewhere.
There has been an unfavourable reaction to our contracts with Great Britain for the sale of our wheat at less than the world price and of the greater part of our other foodstuffs to her to the exclusion of almost every other country.
Here are the remarks heard last Spring by a Canadian travelling through France, Holland. Belgium and Denmark:
(Text):
"Why is it that Canada supplies Britain with wheat at $1.55 and charges us from $2.75 up to $3?" "We, they stated, were your allies during the war equally with Britain, and moreover we endured the hardships and terrors of the German occupation, which Britain did not, and all during that period we continued fighting underground to help you. Why, therefore, are we not entitled to wheat at as cheap a price as you give it to Britain for we are in just as much economic distress and lost to the Germans, cattle, horses and machinery which Britain did not?" "Do you think, they asked, that such an action on the part of Canada is conducive to goodwill in the future when Canada will be looking for markets for her wheat?"
(Translation):
Were it a question of helping the starving nations of Europe, no one would object, as long as we did not go beyond our means, and as long as we considered the need of those who ask for our aid. But Britain is not all Europe. It is not the only starving nation. On the contrary, it is possibly the most fortunate in this regard, according to Red Cross and other reports.
The British Food Minister, Mr. Strachey, stated last October:
(Text):	.
"When I look at the dreadful difficulties in most of Europe today, I think we must have
rMr. Raymond (Beauharnois-Laprairie).]
something to be thankful for in this country." The food situation of western, Europe is far, far more serious than, anything we had to face here.
(Translation):
A bulletin issued by the Information Office of Great Britain stated the following in December 1947:
(Text):
A large section of the people ate better than pre-war ... In 1947, food available for consumption yielded an average of 2,870 calories a day per person . . .
(Translation):
It has been established that the normal ration to feed one person is 2,400 calories. In many countries of Europe, there are millions of people who do not receive half of that normal ration.
Our policy of assistance, as far as that is concerned, is based on the interests of Great Britain and not those of the starving nations.
Practically all of our exports of food products are earmarked for England, who benefits thereby by helping herself first and then making a distribution to other countries at our expense.
Thus does England make friends and strengthens her future trade at our expense.
To rebuild the United Kingdom's economy our own is put in jeopardy.
Now is there any reason to wonder overmuch at the trend of our policy on behalf of British interests, when we know that the Cabinet, whose duty it is to run Canada's business, include five members of Great Britain's Privy Council, namely: our Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), the Minister of Reconstruction and of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner-), who, according to their oaths of office, pledged their word that the empire's interests will be protected and promoted against any country. These are excerpts from the form of oath taken by members of the imperial privy council:
(Text):
I do swear by Almighty God to be a true and faithful servant unto the King's Majesty, as one of His Majesty's Privy Council ... I will to my uttermost bear faith and allegiance unto the King's Majesty, and will assist and defend all jurisdictions, pre-eminences and authorities, granted to His Majesty, and annexed to the crown by acts of parliament, or otherwise, against all foreign princes, persons, prelates, states or potentates. And generally in all things I will do as a faithful and true servant ' ought to do to His Majesty.
(Translation):
Here is a further brief excerpt from the form of oath taken by members of the Canadian Privy Council.

The Address-Mr. M. Raymond
(Text):
You ... do solemnly promise and1 swear that you will serve His Majesty truly and faithfully in the place of his council in this His Majesty's Dominion of Canada ... In general you will be vigilant, diligent, and circumspect in all your doings touching the King's Majesty's affairs.
(Translation):
It should be noted that a member of the Privy Council in Canada is not the equal of a member of the Privy Council in the United Kingdom. The former is styled "Honourable" and the latter "Right Honourable," which seems to indicate the degree of superiority attached to the position.
Our five ministers who are also members of the imperal privy council hold key positions in the Canadian cabinet; in fact they direct the government's policy.
There is first the Prime Minister, whose imperialistic feelings were revealed during and since the war. It was he who in 1941 said in Prince Albert that he had been ready in 1938 to engage Canada in a war in which England *was involved, even at the risk of breaking away from his party, which was divided.
Was he then furthering the interests of Canada or those of the King of England? Were his thoughts those of a member of the Canadian or of the imperial privy council?
What is the explanation for the persistence in maintaining the privy council as an appeal court, for our dependence upon London for amendments to our constitution, for the right of disallowance of our legislation which the Statute of Westminster has not abolished, and finally, for the persistence in appointing as Governor General a stranger, and his refusal to give us a truly distinctive flag. Those are so many colonial ties.
It is not surprising that Mr. Neville Chamberlain, in his memoirs, should have judged our Prime Minister to be "a good and loyal imperialist" and that the King of Great Britain should have awarded him a medal for signal services to the empire.
Then we come to the Minister of Justice who seems to have forgotten the Statute of Westminster.
This right hon. gentleman, stated in this house, in February, 1942, that he was representing in the government those who felt duty bound to fight for the British empire in all parts of the world and, again in 1947, claimed that whenever the economic stability of Great Britain was threatened our national interest was at stake.
Then also there is the Secretary of State for External Affairs who opposed a request of our Canadian bishops for a tax exemption on incomes up to 83,000 a year giving as a reason that the government would be deprived of some $250 million and adding that he 5849-120
preferred to pay the same amount of money as family allowances. If he could forget that he is a member of the Imperial Privy Council, he could grant such an exemption and still afford to pay family allowances, by reducing the disguised gifts made to Great Britain. He would then be acting as a member of the Privy Council for Canada.
As to the Minister of Reconstruction and of Trade and Commerce, his chief concern seems to be the economic reconstruction of the empire. His objective in controlling our exports is to direct them towards the United Kingdom. He is much more anxious to find houses for the people of the British Isles than for our Canadian people. He is truly a loyal member of the Imperial Privy Council.
Finally, the Minister of Agriculture holds the key to the granaries that feed the starving who, in his eyes, are found only in London. He practically gives away our wheat; Canadians must resign themselves to eating cow meat because good beef is sent to Great Britain. During the packers strike of last September, he was less concerned with the plight of Canadian families deprived of meat than with the problem of the British Isles whose inhabitants might miss our deliveries if they were not maintained. His attitude is not surprising since he is a member of the Imperial Privy Council.
What are we to think of this abnormal situation? Some cabinet members are bound by a dual allegiance, having sworn to serve another country as well as their own; that is why Canadian interests are invariably sacrificed to those of the United Kingdom. It is inconceivable that such an anomaly, to say the least, should exist in a sovereign state.
To my mind, Mr. Speaker, the duties of a member of the Canadian Privy Council are incompatible with those of a member of the United Kingdom Privy Council, because it is impossible to serve two masters at a time, the one in America, the other in Europe.
The interests of the two countries are different, as the Prime Minister stated in this house on May 24. 1938. He said:
In times of world disturbance, the policies of no two c-ountzries can be alike, provided they are rooted in their own interests or the ideals in which their interests are sublimated, and 'are not merely echoes of the policies of other countries.
It is therefore obvious that one cannot counsel two parties whose interests are or may be in opposition. May I bring to your attention the statement issued by Lord Tweedsmuir in October, 1937:
Canada, is a sovereign nation . . .
A Canadian's first loyalty is not to the British Commonwealth of Nations but to Canada and Canada's king.
