Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate, realizing that it has been some length of time since it was begun. First, I should like to join with other hon. members in expressing my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I have listened to the various speakers who have taken part in the debate, and it has been somewhat of an education to me to learn something more about this great country which we are pleased to call Canada.
I should like to tell the house something about the county of Northumberland, which I have the honour to represent. It may be of interest to know that it is the important part of Ontario located eighty miles east of Toronto. Cobourg is our largest town. It is an all-year port, with a ferry service plying between that point and the city of Rochester in the United States. Much coal ir delivered to the port of Cobourg, and we hope that at some time ocean-going vessels may call there.
There is no trouble in defining our boundaries, because we have lake Ontario on the south and Rice lake and the Trent river on the north. That part of Ontario is considered as being one of the greatest tourist places in the province, if not in all Canada. If you want good fishing come to Rice lake and the Trent river, because we really have the fish there.
During both wars many of the young men toi my constituency turned out in defence of this country. I am glad to be able to say that many veterans have come back and have re-established themselves in Northumberland county. It was a pleasure for me to sit on the veterans affairs committee. A lot of good work was accomplished at that time. We shall never be finished with our veteran problem as long as there is a veteran living. It is my opinion that we should give the greatest consideration to matters affecting veterans. They should be given the best the country can afford. We have been told of some slight increases that are to be given. I realize that it costs a lot of money when you are dealing, not just with one person but right across the board. However, when we are dealing with veterans, especially those who have lost limbs or are maimed in other ways, we should see that they have no worries in regard to financial matters.
I should like to say something about our transportation systems. We used to hear about railways, seaways and highways. First of all, I should like to say something about our railways in so far as they concern the town of Cobourg and the people in the front

part of Northumberland. The railways have adopted schedules to speed up their trains and for some reason or another they go right through the county of Northumberland with their fast trains. Generally these trains are run in two or three sections. This practice affects other counties along the lake shore, because they leave out many important towns. When there are two or three sections of a train operating daily I see no reason why they could not stagger the schedule to permit one section to stop at some of these important places. That would give service to the people. While the trains have been crowded lately, we can remember back when there was lots of room. If we want this system to pay its way we should give service to the people and encourage railway traffic.
The problem of the St. Lawrence seaway is a large one because it concerns the United States. However, I think some progress should be made. It is claimed that water transportation is the cheapest and, if so, we should make more use of it.
We have in Ontario one of the finest highway systems in the country, but we should think along the lines of a trans-Canada highway so that we can travel from coast to coast on our own highways. The minister who is looking after this matter should try to get the various highway departments together to consider a national scheme.
Taxes are of great concern to most people and the eight per cent sales tax certainly adds considerably to the cost of living. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) could see his way clear to reduce this tax it would make a considerable difference to the family budget. To those in the lower income brackets, the exemptions of $750 and $1,500 are much too low with the present high cost of living. I have had considerable correspondence from people in my riding on this matter. Many of our schoolteachers are getting along on fairly modest salaries and they, with many others in the same class, are finding that the present exemption does not permit them to maintain their standard of living. They think they should have an exemption of $1,200 for single persons and $2,000 for married. I hope the Minister of Finance will give some consideration to these people when he brings down his budget.
I think we all realize that it is difficult to lower taxes unless there is a reduction in the money being spent. Recently I asked for details of the Belleville tax office located in Hastings county. I was told that there were so many employees in that office people could hardly get inside. Some farmers who have

The Address-Mr. Drope
attempted to file income tax forms have said that there seemed to be more employees than there were taxpayers. I was surprised at the return I received this morning. This shows that in 1945 in this small office there were sixty-four employees and that the total collections amounted to $10,680,000. In 1946 there were seventy-seven employees and they collected a little over $10,000,000. In 1947 they had eighty-two employees and their collections were down $3,000,000. In 1948 they had just doubled the number of employees they had in 1945, the present total being 121.
My experience in business has been that when your dollar volume of sales go down y-ou must curtail expenses somewhere else. If *this is a fair example of other offices throughout the land; if they have all doubled their staffs in the last two or three years, we can understand why taxes are not being reduced. I suggest that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) look into this matter. Surely, if they needed only sixty-four employees to collect S10.000,000 in 1945 they do not need 121 employees in 1948.
I think I am entitled to say something about agriculture since I come from a large agricultural counts'. Yesterday and this afternoon wc heard something about apples from the county of Durham. We are just immediately east of the county of Durham. Our apple growers are known as the apple growers of the united counties of Northumberland and Durham. We think we grow just a little better apple than they do in Durham.
Give us a sample.

Someone has suggested that I give samples. I have taken note of what the Speaker has said with regard to no exhibits being produced in the house. Probably he thought I might be bringing in a cow some time. Since he has ruled them out I am unable to present any at the present time, but if any hon. members come around to my office I will see what I can do. The apple producers are certainly putting out a good product. If the apples are merchandised properly and the people realize their food value I think more of them will be used in our country . We all seem to think we must use imported oranges and grapefruit in our diet, but I believe it is likely that the medical men in the house would say that apples would be just as good for our health.
We have had some discussion about the vegetable growers. In the southern part of my county we can grow all the vegetables that a good many cities require, but our farmers are hesitant about going into that heavily without some assurance of a market for what they
5849-120^
produce. I have often seen thousands of perishable vegetables, cabbages and so forth, dumped simply because there was no market for them. If vegetable growers were assured of a market for a reasonable length of time they could produce all the vegetables we require in Canada.
The beef cattle producers in this country seem to think they are being deprived of a valuable market in the United States, where cattle prices are much higher. They feel that we should get some shipments of our beef cattle into the United States market, if only so that the people across the line will not lose their taste for our beef.
There has been talk about improving all the cattle herds in this country. I believe that the system of artificial insemination from improved sires should be encouraged by our departments of agriculture. The T.B. testing of cattle has been carried on in various parts of the country, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) promised me last year that this work would be continued in the county of Northumberland. Just a small fraction of the county was covered by part-time veterinaries, and the work there was only started and has not been completed. I trust that this important work will be completed at the earliest possible moment.
A word about dairy products and their distribution. We are realizing that the best food value we can get for our dollar today is what is spent on dairy products. Milk is accepted as one of the best foods a person can use. A great many of our farmers, particularly in the southern part of my county are supplying milk to the Toronto market and other centres. In the eastern and northern parts of my county we have many cheese factories. The cheese industry means more to this country than the average person appreciates. It is one of the main dairy products that we can successfully export, and one of the things that the British people are always desirous of getting is good Canadian cheese.
We consume in this country all the butter that we can produce, and in the next four or five weeks a butter distribution problem will arise, because of the ceiling that has been put on butter. Butter is the only dairy product on which the ceiling has been reimposed. That has held u,p the movement of butter from one province to another. The only place where there is any surplus butter today is in western Canada, and it is found only in small lots, probably fifty to one hundred boxes. In order to ship this to eastern markets like Toronto and Montreal, it would have to be assembled in carload lots, about 400 boxes to a car
The Address-Mr. Quelch

Assembling this butter from small lots into carload lots involves considerable expense and, because of the ceiling on butter, the shipper is unable to recover that expense. Therefore it seems to me that it would be of benefit to the consumers of Canada if the department concerned would see that financial help was given in assembling this butter for delivery to eastern markets, where it will be needed for a few weeks before our spring production comes on.
International affairs are of grave concern to all of us. We should not be like the ostrich, hiding our heads in the sand. We can all see something of what is taking place abroad. Only this afternoon two or three members urged that time be found to have a debate on international affairs in this house. Whatever procedure may be followed, we should certainly be doing something to work out a solution of international problems that would avoid another world conflict, which would cause so much suffering and hardship and destruction. We all sincerely hope that it will not be necessary for the cream of our youth, our young men and our young women, to come forward again to fight in another world war. Surely wiser counsels can prevail. The only thing is to face up to the problem and while we yet have time, take decisive measures which seem to be wise.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment to the amendment moved by the C.C.F. reads as follows:
That the following words be inserted:
This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to use the powers provided by parliament to control prices, and by their actions have caused alarming increases in the cost of living and a dangerous lowering of the Living standards of the Canadian people.
We feel that the government deserves severe criticism for allowing the price of farm machinery to rise sharply while controlling the prices of other commodities. I mention machinery specifically, because I think it was the action of the wartime prices and trade board in allowing a 12J per cent increase in the price of machinery in 1946 which, first of all, discredited that board in the eyes of the people.
Furthermore, we criticize the government for raising the price of commodities by increasing indirect taxation. The government must bear a substantial part of the blame for high prices due to the high tax content therein, thereby, of course, lowering the standard of living of people in the low-income groups. For that reason we intend to support the amendment to the amendment.
But I want to make it clear that, while we
support the C.C.F. amendment, we do not sup-

port them in their demand1 for the reimposition of all price controls and the rolling back of prices to the 1946 level. We believe that such a policy at this time would create a great deal of confusion. We believe, further, that it would tend to discourage many lines of production and, in addition, would mean a substantial increase in taxation. My reason for saying that is this. In 1947 our exports, according to the report of the Bank of Canada, were in the neighbourhood of $2,800 million. Our imports were in an amount close to that. At the same time, the price of goods outside Canada was considerably higher than the price level within Canada. Therefore, if you are to roll back prices to the 1946 level it will be necessary heavily to subsidize all your imported goods. Iu addition, you would have to subsidize the price of agricultural products if you were to roll them back to 1946; or, on the other hand, of course, get the farmers to take a reduction in price. It is quite obvious that subsidies of those dimensions would mean a heavy increase in taxation at this time.
Some people may argue that we have a fairly substantia! surplus of $600 million or $700 million or more, and1 we could use that surplus for that purpose. On the other hand, most hon. members are advocating a substantial increase in old age pensions, a reduction in indirect taxation, and an increase in the income tax exemption. All hon. members will agree, I believe, that this would more than wipe out any surplus that we may have. If it was the intention to roll back prices to the 1946 level it would mean a very heavy program of subsidization that would be bound to increase taxation, and at this time the people are not asking for increased taxation.
Ever since this group first came into the house in 1936, we have consistently expressed the opinion that it should be the responsibility of the federal government to adjust prices to a level that would be fair to both the consumer and the producer. We all know that the secondary industries have always been in the position where they could sell their products so as to recover costs of production and earn a fair profit. But unfortunately that has not been the position in the primary industries. They generally find that they have to take world prices. In spite of the fact that, with the exception of wheat, over ninety per cent of our agricultural products in the past was consumed in Canada, the ten per cent that was exported invariably set the price of the ninety per cent that was consumed in this country. We all remember only too well what the farmers went through in the thirties as a result of that type of policy. Therefore we have always insisted

The Address-Mr. Quelch
1SS1
that the federal government must assume responsibility for guaranteeing to the primary producers a fair price; and by a fair price I mean a price that will return to the farmer his fair share of the national income, so that the price of agricultural products will bear a fair relationship to the price of other commodities.
We have also urged that the federal government should adjust the price of consumer goods, so that the aggregate of prices of consumer goods would balance with the effective purchasing power of the people. We maintain that only in that way can you hope to maintain your production at an optimum level, because no industry can continue to produce unless it can sell. We therefore maintain that it should1 be the responsibility of the government at all times to maintain an effective demand against the production in the country.
During the war and in the immediate postwar years, special price controls and rationing were necessary, on account of the needs of war; but the time will come in the very near future when it will be necessary to take action to maintain an effective demand against our production. That warning was given to the country by Graham Towers in his 1946 report.
It seems to me that, during this debate, there has been an air of unreality about a number of speeches that have been made on economic conditions in Canada. The impression has been created that we are climbing up an unending road and that we are apt to collapse en route, when in reality the situation is that we are climbing a hill, the top of which may be reached at any time, and then the great danger that will face the country is that we may come down the other side so fast that we shall not be able to stop to level off at the point we would want to, but, instead of that, we may very well crash at the bottom into a depression.
AVe were given a very fair picture of the situation by the governor of the Bank of Canada in his 1946 report. We were given the same picture by the former minister of finance in his 1946 budget, and again we were warned of the situation by the United States economist Beardsley Ruml. Briefly the situation explained to us was this: the immediate post-war years would be inflationary years due mainly to three things: first, to the fact that there was a large backlog of demand created by unspent war savings; second, to the amount of money that would be paid out for reconversion, and, third, to the fact that large foreign credits were being granted, and therefore goods exported under these credits without any imports being brought back in return.
As a result of these things, there would unquestionably be an inflationary trend in this country. But at the same time, when the governor of the Bank of Canada warned us of the situation he also warned that, after that, the main problem which would be facing the country would be to maintain a demand for production.
Some hon. members have ridiculed the idea of prices levelling off. They say we are in the third year of peace; it is the third year since the war and prices have not levelled off. They also suggested that these people who were advocating the lifting of price controls apparently thought prices would immediately level off. I do not believe any hon. member who was advocating that price ceilings should, be lifted thought for one minute that prices would immediately level off. It is quite evident that this would take time.
When I spoke in the house last year I quoted the statement of Beardsley Ruml. Beardsley Ruml indicated that everything pointed to the fact that prices would first break or first show a falling off in the spring of 1948. He made that statement in the spring of 1947. I think his prophecy was a very good one, because we have already seen a break in the price structure, and the extent to which prices will break further will depend largely upon the type of action that is taken in the United States and in this country. If no action were taken there would probably be a further break; but, on the other hand, if large credits are granted under the Marshall plan, no doubt these prices will be maintained. AVhat I cannot understand is this: some people are not ready to wait for a depression to come; they apparently want to push us into one. So far as the experience of Canadians is concerned, most people in this country have suffered far more through depressions than they have through booms. When I recall the thirties and the poverty and degradation that so many people went through, how they lost their life savings, their life insurance, their farms, even their health, and, in some cases, even their lives, I cannot understand people in this country today continually talking as though they were hoping for a depression to come in the near future to bring prices down. I realize that, at a time like this, when we have high prices there are people in the low-income groups who are suffering and suffering severely. We are of the opinion, and we have said so, that government should take immediate action to look after the people in low-income groups, such as old age pensioners and other classes to whom I shall refer later on.
The Address-Mr. Quelch

I wish to say a few words regarding the increased cost of living. The C.C.F. group blames profiteering mostly for the increased cost of living. There is no doubt that part of the reason for the tinereased cost of living is profiteering, since we are still in an inflationary period, and any time you have an inflationary period anybody who has anything to sell tries to get a little bit more, whether it be for his labour or for his commodity. Everybody is out to try to get the highest price for what he has to sell; but it is amazing how many people with high incomes criticizing the high cost of living today do not realize that their own income is part and parcel of the high price level. Therefore, if a fall in the price level occurs, their income will go down as well. I think a very good example of that is given by the governor of the Bank of Canada in his 1917 report on page 19:
The combined effect of upward pressure on our price level from foreign and domestic sources was to increase the general wholesale price index by 28 per cent, and the cost of living index by 15 per cent during 1947. Although the situation with respect to wage nates varied considerably among different groups of wage earner's, average hourly earnings of hourlyrated employees in manufacturing industry rose by about 15 per cent for the year, and their average weekly earnings increased by nearly 16 per cent.
Note that an increase in wages gave rise to an increase in the cost of living. The wage earner, however, does not appreciate that his increase in wages is part of the increased prices.
We in the Social Credit party have always emphasized the fact that you cannot increase the purchasing power of the people by increasing wages, because when you increase wages prices will rise and absorb the benefits of the increased wage. We have always emphasized the fact that if you want to increase the purchasing power of the people it will be necessary to supplement the wage earner's income by additional payments outside the industrial system.
Now the Conservative party, or perhaps I should say the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), who, I believe, is the financial critic for the Conservative party, lays special emphasis on the dangers of inflation. He has referred on a number of occasions to the fact that at the present time the money supply in Canada is three times what it was in 1939, and he has time and again criticized the government for their inflationary policy. With all kindness I would say to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario that if he

is going to criticize any party in this house for that situation he should turn his criticism on his own party.
Let me explain what I mean. He quoted with approval the statement by the then minister of finance in 1939 to the effect that, as soon as we had reached the point of full employment, it would not be wise to have a further expansion of money. He quoted that as I said with approval. I would like to refer him to the attitude of the Conservative party in this house in the first year in which there was a substantial increase in taxation, the year 1942. In 1942 when we were discussing the budget proposal in this house, the then leader of the Conservative party criticized bitterly .the proposals for an increase in taxation and suggested that there might be an easier way of financing the war, and he said, "Page the member for Lethbridge". He was apparently advocating that, instead of financing the war by increased taxation, we should finance it by national money.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

I want to ask the hon. member if he is aware that, while I did, as he has stated, speak in approval of the budget speech of 1939, in its hope that it might be able shortly to stop the extension of credit, I went on to point out that at that time we had a phony war, which we hoped would last only a short time. I also indicated that I thought that, with the enormous expansion which came during the war, the steps, though undoubtedly inflationary, taken during the war, were justified up to the end of the war. My criticism rested on what had taken place since that time.

Nevertheless the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario has referred time and again to the fact that we now have three times as much money in circulation as in 1939. The government's war policy, its financial policy, was pay as you go as far as possible; and yet, when the government of the day tried as far as it could to put into effect a pay-as-you-go policy, the most bitter criticism came from the Conservative party regarding taxation. And, mind you, they went farther than that. They took the stand that if the government were not prepared to adopt some such proposals as those of the hon. member for Lethbridge, they should curtail the war effort to a stipulated amount of money.

Before the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I had been discussing the question of whose was the responsibility for increasing the supply of money during the war. I think we all agree that the expansion of money which took place at that time was essential in order to maintain the volume of production that was required. For the same reason we feel that the present supply of money will also be necessary if we are to maintain production at its maximum level. When you discuss the danger of inflation you must ask, what is. the best solution of the problem of inflation? I would say the best solution is the expansion of production; and if we are to expand production in this country we must maintain an easy-money policy.
I understand that when the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario spoke a few days ago- and I intend to refer to this only briefly, because I understand that the hon. member has to be absent from the house this evening-he suggested that we should increase interest rates at this time. I shall discuss that suggestion some other time; but, in passing, I should like to make this comment. If at the present time it is desirable that we should expand production in this country- and I do not think anyone will deny that statement-then would it be wise to adopt a tight-money policy? Would it be wise to increase the cost of money, thereby increasing the basic cost of production? When you increase interest rates you do increase the basic cost of production; and how can we hope to compete with the other nations of
The Address-M r. Quelch

the world in production if we are going out of our way to increase the basic cost of that production?
I have referred briefly to the C.C.F. contention that profiteering was largely responsible for the increase in prices, and also to the references of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario to the danger of inflation. I would say that in my opinion one of the principal causes of the increase in prices is the fact that Canada is and has been a heavy exporter and importer of goods. As I pointed out, last year we exported in the neighbourhood of $2,800 million worth of goods, and imported goods to a similar amount. Price levels outside Canada are higher than in Canada. Therefore, Canada being a heavy exporter and importer, the price level in this country is bound to rise unless we are going to indulge in a heavy program of subsidization. I know it may be argued that we were able to control prices during the war, and that, therefore, there is no reason why we should not be able to control them at this time. I should like to remind hon. members that during the war we paid heavy subsidies; we maintained heavy taxation; we borrowed heavily, and we imposed rigid controls. I do not believe for one moment that the people of Canada today would tolerate the continuation of such a policy, because on all sides we hear people demanding that there be a reduction in taxation.
The main criticism we hear today is with respect to prices of farm produce. That is only natural. People compare the price level of agricultural produce today with the price level in 1939, and they find that the increase in prices of agricultural products is greater than the increase in other commodities. That is natural, of course; and the reason is that, in the thirties, prices of agricultural products were altogether too low in comparison with prices of other commodities, so what has taken place has been merely a slight levelling up in the relationship between prices of agricultural goods and prices of other commodities. Furthermore, when people criticize agricultural prices today they forget the tremendous losses agriculture suffered in the thirties. Those losses can be made up only by agriculture receiving prices that will not only meet the cost of production but will also return a fair profit.
I understand that the C.C.F. and quite a number of other people favour the payment of subsidies in order to reduce prices of agricultural products to the consumer. I say, why pick on agricultural products? The moment you commence to subsidize agricultural products, people will get the impression that
	|
agricultural prices are too high in relation to prices of other commodities. Furthermore, why should we sell agricultural products at less than the cost of production, to people in the high-income brackets? Look at the people who today are receiving large incomes, people who are selling their own products at high prices. Why should they be allowed to buy agricultural products at less than the cost of production? So personally I am opposed to subsidizing the consumer at this time to permit him to buy agricultural products at lower prices, because immediately people will get the impression that agricultural prices are too high.
We in this group believe in subsidies; we always have believed in them, but for a different purpose. First of all, we believe in subsidies for the purpose of establishing a basic income, raising the income of the people in the low-income brackets to a level which will permit them to live decently. Then we have advocated for a long time that the old age pension should be increased to $50 a month. In the first place, we should reduce the age from seventy to sixty-five; then, as production increased in relation to demand, we could reduce it further to sixty. We recognized the need of paying pensions to people who are blind; and we reduced the age to twenty-one. We advocated this because these people are largely physically incapacitated. But I could never understand why we drew the line at people who are blind. Surely the people who are totally disabled from other causes need pensions just as much as the people who are blind, and I think it is high time the government brought down a policy whereby pensions would be paid to all people physically incapacitated. Another way of taking care of people in the low-income brackets-and I am referring to these people because they are the ones who are suffering today as a result of the high prices, not the people in the high-income brackets, who can easily afford the higher prices-would be to increase the rate of family allowances; and to the extent that those in the high-income brackets did not need this help, the income tax would deprive them of it.
Then, let us take the question of disability pensions for veterans, and the war veterans allowance. I understand that the government has agreed to increase the disability pensions by sixteen per cent. That is all to the good; but, generally speaking, the veterans' organizations consider that the increase should be at least twenty-five per cent. In view of the fact that we shall be discussing this matter in the house in the near future I am not going

to say more on this question, but at the moment I should like to say a word on the war veterans allowance, which was introduced as a recognition of the fact that the veteran had pre-aged by ten years, and should, therefore, be given a pension at sixty instead of at seventy. Well, today we find that people in receipt of the war veterans allowance are getting less than the old age pensioners. Most members of this house are, I think, acquainted with many pitiful cases of people in receipt of war veterans allowance, who are finding it practically impossible to exist. So, when this matter comes up in the house I hope the government will find it possible to wipe out the means test; or, if they are not prepared to wipe it out, at least let the veteran have an income equal to the amount of the exemption under the income tax. Why not try to make the income tax exemption the basic income level to which we shall try to raise all incomes?
Now, of course, the question comes up as to whether we can afford to do this. Just before six o'clock I praised the government for their war policy, under which they said they would not allow any financial restrictions to handicap the war effort. They subscribed to the idea that anything physically possible and desirable could be made financially possible. If that were true in war it can be equally true today. We fought the war to defeat the enemy and to bring into being the new social order we heard so much about those days. If we were prepared to adopt a realistic financial policy to achieve that objective then, how much more important it is that we should maintain a sound policy in these times in order to win the peace for which we fought and sacrificed so dearly.
There has always been an excuse in the past for doing nothing. In the thirties we were told we could not do this or that for the simple reason that we had not the money. No one suggested for one moment in those days that we had not the goods. In those days we had 500.000 unemployed. Our industries were running at less than fifty per cent of capacity. It would have been a simple matter to put the unemployed to work and to provide the things the people needed; but we were told we could not do that because we could not get the money. It took a war to waken the government to what could be done under a realistic financial policy.
The people expressed amazement that, as a result of a changed financial policy, we were able in a short space of time to double the country's production. But those same people are now taking it for granted that we must

have reduced production. I think the government will find it pretty hard to give us an excuse today for not making anything that is physically possible and desirable financially possible. I should like to hear the reasons. If war were declared tomorrow-and we hope it will not be for many years-would the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) suggest for one moment that the government would reverse its former war policy? I would again remind the house of the position about which the governor of the Bank of Canada warned us, a position where the present under-production, will expand and we shall not be able to maintain an effective demand against that production. That time will come. The governor of the Bank of Canada warned us it would come. We have already seen a price break, and this may be a warning that that situation may come in the near future. When that situation develops, then we maintain that it will be the responsibility -of ihe government to establish a policy which will make it possible to maintain an effective demand against our production at all times. When that time comes we believe the government will be justified in paying a price discount on the price of all goods to the extent necessary to balance demand with supply.
For example, if the demand is only 90 per cent of supply, then the government would be justified in paying to an industry a ten per cent discount on its sales of goods so as to equate demand and supply. Industry would be able to sell goods at a ten per cent discount. The sales slips would be taken to the bank and a credit of ten per cent would be allowed, the bank being reimbursed by the government. In that way at all times there would be a balance so as to equate demand with supply.
Furthermore, in order to maintain a high level of production, the government must guarantee parity prices to the farmer. For the past eight years the farmers have been required to sell for less than they could have, due to a policy of government intervention. Then, for a period of ten years before the war they had to sell at world market prices, which were then low. Therefore the farmers have every right and justification for demanding that in future, as a basic principle, they should receive a guaranteed price, and that that guaranteed price should be based upon parity, that is a price which would bear a fair relationship to prices of other commodities. The federal government should reorganize the Agricultural Prices Support Act, so that it would be made a permanent piece of legislation. And it should be made quite clear under that act that prices to be paid in the future will be parity prices.
The all-important question today is that of maintaining a maximum degree of production. As I have already pointed out, the 
best way to end inflation is to increase the production of consumer goods so as to satisfy demand. But we insist that one of the chief deterrents to increased production is indirect taxation. It increases costs 'to the producer, while at the same time increasing costs to the consumer. Furthermore, we feel that the government should increase the rate of exemptions from income tax. That is probably the best way to encourage labour and also to encourage the farmer to increase production.
While I am on the subject of taxation, I should like to say a few words regarding the prairie farmers' income tax form. I happened to see it only the other night and I have felt bitter ever since reading it. This is supposed to be a simplified form. I am not taking any special exception on that score. It is a bigger form. But what I am taking definite exception to is what appears at page 6, where it asks for the farmer's net worth statement. I believe farmers will bitterly resent this form, particularly this page, as being discriminatory action against them.
On this page the farmer is required to show the cash on his person at December 31, 1947, and December 31, 1946. He is also required to show cash in bank, cash in safety deposit boxes, the amount of government bonds and shares that he has either on the farm or, apparently, in a safety deposit box.
I would draw this fact to the attention of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), that no other occupational group is required to disclose this information. Then, if no other occupational group is required to provide this information, why should the farmer be required to do so? I have been told by certain officials that the reason is that they have to catch up with the farmer. That is the reason given by some of the officials. In other words, they are insinuating that the farmers are more dishonest than other groups. Let me say to the minister I am satisfied that the farmers of this country are just as honest as the members of the profession he represents, or those of any other profession.
So am I.

Then, why insinuate that the farmers are not honest, by requiring that this form be filled out? By doing that, you are definitely insinuating that the farmers are not honest. And I, as a farmer member of parliament, bitterly resent the fact that I am required to fill out that information, information which any other member of parliament who is not a farmer does not have to fill out.
I suggest to the minister that, even though this form has been sent out, it would be a

good thing for his department to notify the farmers that whether they fill out the information on that page or not is purely optional. If it is made optional I do not think there would be any objection. You say to me, "You do not need to fill it in unless you want to," and I would not mind filling it in, but when you tell me that I have to fill it in when nobody else has to fill it in, then you accuse me of being dishonest and I resent the imputation.
Before taking my seat, I should like to say a few words with regard to my constituency. The constituency which I represent in east central Alberta is sparsely populated. Over 70 per cent of the original settlers have left because of drought conditions. Surveys of an irrigation project known as the Red Deer diversion have been completed and approved. This project provides for the irrigation of 500,000 acres. The land is good, and services have already been established in the area in the form of roads, railways, towns and schools. The project would make it possible for the district to support an additional population of over 30,000 people.
Canada has embarked upon an expanding immigration program and Europeans would be ideally adapted to settling on irrigated farms. Therefore, in closing, I urge upon the government the desirability of going ahead immediately with the construction of that project in order to make self-supporting a large area which could help other countries by providing homes for people in displaced persons camps.

If you want more recent evidence of it look at the statement made in the house by the Prime Minister last week in which he said he would ask this house to adjourn on June 30 whether the business of the country and of parliament was concluded or not, in order that the Liberal party might unimpeded hold its national convention this summer. The interests of the party first, the interests of the country and the parliament second-that is the record of this government all the way through. They have always got an excuse for situations arising out of their own dilatoriness, as we have seen very recently. Here is the latest episode, the attempt to impose taxation without any reference to parliament, the levying of imposts in the form of taxes before parliament is even in session to hear the minister's announcement. Yes, Mr. Speaker, well may we recall the words of William Pitt:
Necessity is the plea for every infringement of human freedom. It is the argument of tyrants; it is the creed of slaves.
Those who want to submit to that can cheer the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to the echo, if they like. I note the applause of the Minister of Finance by those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker.
It is high time that this government was told that government is not to be carried on any longer simply by wise-cracking. We expect something more serious from government than the way in which it has been carried on of late from the government benches.
Let us recall the Declaration of Right, 1628, and the Bill of Rights, 1689, with their assertion of the right of parliament and parliament alone to levy taxes and their denial to the executive branch of government of any right to impose levies of any kind without the authority of parliament. This government has torn them up, just as in earlier days it tore up the rights of Canadians under Magna Carta. With all this has gone the breaking of the government's promises. I do not need to remind you, Mr. Speaker, of the way in which the government recently tore up the representations made to this house by the present Minister of Justice two years ago when the foreign exchange control bill was introduced. What has been the best the government has been able to do? The best has been to offer quibbles through the Minister of Finance to try to find some minute distinction between a statement of the government
The Address-Mr. Fleming

and an undertaking by the government. Apparently undertakings by the government have some greater validity than mere statements. Therefore we are on our guard in this chamber, that mere statements by members of the government, speaking with the full authority of the government, are not to be regarded by the house as binding on the government when it suits the government's purpose to ignore them.
When we are talking about the preservation of freedom in parliament let us be on our guard against the attempts that are being made under the guise of this delightful expression "planning" to foist socialism on this country, because the socialists find that the word "socialism" has not the appeal that they thought it had in 1933 and 1934, and so now they are calling it planning.
Well, planning is not all confined to the C.C.F. An exponent of planning is today a member of the government, the government leader in the senate. Speaking for the Liberal party on free time over the CBC, last August 6, Senator Wishart Robertson said this:
My guess is that any future government in Canada, whatever its political complexion, will resort to some type of economic planning.
Hear, hear.

Of course the C.C.F. will applaud that; of course they will. It is right down their alley; and these vociferous people to your right, Mr. Speaker, who are applauding, are falling right into the hands of the C.C.F. Unfortunately they are so blind that they do not see they are on the slippery slide into socialism. They are just playing into the hands of the socialists, if only they could see it. They are the people who are contributing so much to the inroads of socialism in this country. Do not let anyone ever think that you can play fast and loose with this economic planning without risking the loss of individual freedom.
Oh nuts!

I will only remind some forgetful gentlemen down yonder of the words of Mr. Laski who was chairman of the executive of the British labour party and who not so many months ago expressed doubt-these are his words-"whether in a period of transition to socialism a labour government"-by which, of course, he meant a socialist government- "could risk the overthrow of its measures as a result of a general election." It is no historical accident that modern individual freedom, conceived m terms of our parliamentary institutions and the duty of parliament to stand as the guardian of the rights of the individual, has grown hand in hand with our modern 
system of free enterprise. You knock the props out from under any system of free enterprise and do not delude yourself that you can hold on to individual freedom; you cannot.
Down with the props.

In the amendment to the amendment there is the suggestion that the time has come to reimpose certain controls. Everyone who will be frank about this knows perfectly well that you cannot have an overall system of price control without controlling wages and salaries, and we of the Progressive Conservative party are absolutely, flatly and resolutely opposed to the state stepping in and putting ceilings on wages. We will fight that, and we are fighting against the sort of thing that is going on in the United Kingdom today in the form of direction of labour, the first time since parliamentary institutions and cabinet government came into effect in the old country that you have direction of labour in time of peace.
Everybody is working.

They are working, are they? Let anybody leave his employment who is not engaged in agriculture or coal mining today and where does he go? He has to go to a government bureau and they will put him in coal mining or agriculture. That is how the control over manpower is enforced. An Associated Press dispatch from London of October 3, which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail of October 4, says this:
Directed labour must take jobs. Isaacs warns.
Labour Minister Isaacs warned today that workers who become "sticky and nasty" when directed to a job under Britain's new manpower regulations would be told, "You will have this one, whether you like it or not."
Is that freedom? It is socialism.
Did you ever hear of direction of labour under the Unemployment Insurance Act?

Anyone who has followed the tortuous course of the socialists, knows that those of the socialist creed are bound to regard the constitution of Canada, with its division of powers as between the dominion and the provinces, as a bar to socialism. That is why they are the sworn enemies of the federal system in this country. But they do not stop there. They regard the courts which are, of course, the interpreters of the constitution, the interpreters of the law of this country, as a bar to their aims. It is only natural that the Premier of Saskatchewan should have attacked the courts, as he did on January 14, complaining that these courts were

The Address-Mr. Fleming
giving judgments adverse to the government of Saskatchewan. That kind of speech might well have been made by any fascist or any communist.
Read the speech.

The idea that the courts should be criticized was because, as the Premier of Saskatchewan said, "We have collided head-on with the courts." He criticized them as not having fought on the side of the government. He said that the government was fighting on the side of the people and they were running slam-bang against the courts all the time. Well he might run into the courts, because they are interpreting the laws of this country, although not to the liking of the executive branch of government in that province; interpreting the constitution, but not to the liking of the socialists in that province, and of course the socialists, in consequence, attacked the courts. The courts were the subject of the first attacks by the nazis in Germany.
Then there is the freedom of the press. The freedom of the press is the sort of thing that is a thorn in the side of the socialists, as you see them attacking it through the inquiry into the press of the old country today, and also on the part of those neo-socialists whom you find masquerading under Liberal colours.
Hear, hear.

Neo-socialists masquerading under the Liberal colours. That is why you were surprised, I am sure, at the dangers to the freedom of the press in this country when you learned that certain journalists were recently arrested in Ontario and carried west under the nose of the Minister of Justice, if 3'ou please.
By socialists, I suppose.

Nothing was done about it by the minister.
It is only natural to expect, too, that the government that is tarred with the socialist brush and is seeking to perpetuate itself in office would bring the civil service into itn political orbit. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this government has been using distinguished members of the diplomatic service and senior officers of the civil service to serve the ends of the Liberal party. I have before me a publication called "Politique." It is issued by the National Liberal Federation with headquarters at 172 Wellington street, Ottawa. The committee in charge is composed of Joseph A. Blanchette, a member of this house, Georges-E. Lapalme, M.P., Guy Roberge, M.P.P., Me. Leon Lalande, Me. Jean-Marie Nadeau.
We are told on the cover that this is a publication coming out four times a year, issued by the National Liberal Federation. Here is volume 1, No. 1, and what do we find? The very first article is entitled "L'Ame du Canada devant l'histoire", and this is written by Mr. Edmond Turcotte, who is described as consul general of Canada at Chicago. In this article-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Does the hon. member assert that that was written after Mr. Turcotte was appointed consul general in Chicago?

Mr. Speaker, I am
saying-
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Is he not aware that this manuscript was delivered before Mr. Turcotte was appointed?
This publication was published this winter, 1948. It is dated 1948.
Published, not written.

And the author of this article is described, as he then was, as consul general at Chicago. But that is not all.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Is it a fact that the hon. member does not know that manuscript was prepared by Mr. Turcotte while he was still editor of the journal Le Canada in Montreal?

I am glad the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said what he has, because it reflects all the more seriously and shamefully on this Liberal federation that published it. If on the eve of this man's appointment to the diplomatic service of the country the Liberal federation got him to write such an article and then published the article after his appointment as consul general it is even more shameful.
And that is not all. This same party has other publications as well. Here we have one entitled "The Canadian Liberal," whatever that is. It is called "A Survey of National Affairs, volume 1 No. 2, winter 1948". It is also published by the National Liberal Federation with offices at 172 Wellington street in this city. The editorial advisory board consists of: Hon. Norman Lambert, Hon. Gray Turgeon, Hon. Charles Bishop, John Stirrett,
K.C., II. E. Kidd, Esq., Mrs. Nancy Hodges, M.L.A., and J. Gordon Fogo, Iv.C. There is an article entitled "Jobs for All," written by Arthur MacNamara-not the leader of the band, but the deputy minister of labour, a senior civil servant-in a publication put out by the National Liberal Federation of Canada. This represents a shameful prostitution of the
The Address-Mr. Fleming

civil service of the country. It is a shameful prostitution of the diplomatic service and the senior civil service of the country to serve the ends of the Liberal party.
I have not the time, Mr. Speaker, to go into some of the subjects that I wished to discuss. I should have liked to say something about the shameful record of the government in the matter of housing, the shameful breach of promises, the repudiation of promises by the government, great glowing promises on which they were elected in 1945. Now that these promises have served their purpose of getting the government elected, of course they repudiate them.
Take the treatment of veterans under the Veterans Land Act. I urge the new Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg), who has fallen heir to a sad legacy in that department in connection with the Veterans Land Act administration, to read the revelations of scandal in that administration, exposed in the public accounts committee last summer, which were debated in this house last July 16, beginning at page 5795 of Hansard-the exposure of a situation that is nothing short of a scandal in, this country.
Of course the government saw fit to dispose of the director of the Veterans Land Act after the former minister of veterans affairs, Mr. Mackenzie, that night stood up and defended him to the hilt and said that the charges against him were so much twaddle. They fired him, and now the new director is saying, "The thing to do is to have the Veterans Land Act do a better job of public relations and tell our story to the people."
I have time to say two things in this regard. In this matter of telling the Canadian people, I hope the Veterans Land Act administration will strive to have a very much better record to put before the Canadian people than hitherto. Before they go out with a program of informing the public, I hope they will have a better story to tell; and, in the second place, I hope that if there is any semblance of a sense of fair play left in the government they will give the veterans who are affected the same opportunity of putting their story before the public.
The government denied us the reasonable request for a royal commission last year. They rejected it contemptuously. These veterans are clamouring for an, opportunity to tell their story, and the reason they have not been given that opportunity is that the government has steadfastly and obstinately refused them the opportunity in the one way in which the veterans could have told their story, namely,

to a royal commission. It is a thousand shames to the government who have betrayed the veterans.
It is quite apparent that this government is falling apart. Of course we are coming closer to the national Liberal convention in August. Now here is the Minister of Finance having his department issue statements about this great current budget surplus of $750 million, and along comes another contender for the crown, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and punctures the balloon. He says, "Oh, well, that is not a real surplus at all. You have to take out all the loans we are making; we shall not be repaid these". And so, by that jab, he cuts that surplus by about $500 million. That was not a very kind thing for one rival candidate to do to another, was it, Mr. Speaker?
The Minister of Agriculture has been conducting quite a campaign. He has been running up and down the country discussing immigration, and in Toronto he said this:
Canada should set its immigration objective at 500,000 a year and within ten years increase it to 1,000,000 a year. We can more than double our population in fifteen years.
And there was the Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie, who has now gone to his last resting place in the senate, who stated on October 3, in Toronto:
We should aim for 25,000,000 immigrants in the next twenty-five years.
Apparently the Minister of Agriculture wishes to bring all the immigrants he can into this country, but there is the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and of other portfolios, saying at the same time, "How can Premier Drew do this sort of thing under our nose? It is an impossibility to bring in people in the way the Ontario government are doing." And there is the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) going all the way to Halifax today, looking over the steamer Aquitania to see if he can find room in her for a few immigrants.
This is the month of March, 1948, and the government is talking with such a variety' of voices on the issue of immigration. This government is just falling apart. The leadership contest is on.

And now, I should like to say a few words in French, mother tongue of His Honour the Speaker, and that too of some ancestors of mine who were born in the beautiful province of Quebec.

The time has come when the Canadian parliament must readjust its thinking in keeping with sound Canadian principles. Nearly three years after the war the philosophy of dictatorship, which took hold on the federal government during the war, still prevails at Ottawa. Interference by the Ottawa bureaucrats with the affairs of the people has jeopardized the political rights and the economic future of Canadians.
Last November the Ottawa government, after sitting back idly for seventeen months and watching our supply of United States dollars melt away, announced measures so drastic and so dictatorial that they place all business in Canada at the mercy of the government. One minister wields more power than has been possessed by any man in the history of this country. He may grant import licences to some and refuse them to others. He has been given the power to bring businesses to ruin with the complete loss of the life's savings of many small businessmen.
The Progressive Conservative party says that no such vast powers should be given to any government or any minister. The Canadian parliament should be ashamed to abdicate in favour of a dictatorship.
The government announced heavy new taxes in a radio broadcast made by the Minister of Finance last November 17. He did so without any authority from parliament. Only parliament has the right to authorize the levying of taxes. The government at Ottawa has defied parliament and torn the constitution into ribbons.
This is the same government which is so ready to over-ride the constitutional powers of the provinces and to centralize more and more power and authority at Ottawa at the expense of the provinces. The Progressive Conservative party has consistently and resolutely opposed this centralizing movement, for it is a direct challenge to the freedoms of the Canadian people. If these trends under the present Liberal government toward dictatorship, toward abrogation of the rights of parliament, toward the imposition of taxes without authority of parliament, toward centralization of power at the expense of the provinces, toward the reduction of the constitution to a scrap of paper-if these trends continue they can result sooner or later only in a socialistic
tyranny. The Progressive Conservative party will fight these trends without compromise and I am confident it will in the end win its battle.

In a word, Mr. Speaker, this government has been in office too long. It has forgotten to be responsible to parliament; it has forgotten to be responsible to the people of Canada. Its attitude toward the people today is, "Well, don't we rule them?"
There is only one way of settling this issue; that is, to leave it to the people of Canada. This government has allowed three constituencies to remain without representation. Why? Is the weather adverse again, as it was last year? We are not asking simply that there be by-elections in those three constituencies to permit them to be represented in this house. Our challenge to this government is to let this issue go to the people in a general election at once.

Mr. Speaker, it is expected that in a few minutes we shall be asked to record our vote on the immediate question before us. I am rising now to take just a moment of the time of the house to state the position we find it necessary to take in connection with the amendment to the amendment.
The main motion before the house is the motion always moved at the opening of a parliament, on behalf of the government; a motion to approve the policies and administration of the government. This party moved an amendment to that motion, whieh reads:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's advisers do not possess the confidence of the Canadian, people.
To that amendment a further amendment was moved by the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), in these words:
This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have flailed1 to, use the powers provided by parliament to control prices, and by their actions have caused alarming increases in the cost of living and a dangerous lowering of the living standards of the Canadian, people.
Under our procedure the amendment to the amendment must be voted upon first. That is the first motion upon which we shall be asked to record our votes. With respect to this amendment I want to say that if one word in it had been altered this party could have supported it wholeheartedly. That is the word "prices" in the third line. If instead of "control prices" the amendment had said "control inflation" we could have supported it. That is, if it had read:
This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to use the powers provided by parliament to control inflation . . .
The Address-Mr. Bracken

If it had read in that way we could have supported it. But, as the amendment to the amendment now reads, while it expresses the views of the members of the party whose leader moved it-and I respect them for the views they hold-it carries the implication that by controlling prices-to use am example, by controlling prices of farm products at a time when costs of production are mot controlled-we could thus keep down the cost of living. We cannot subscribe to that thesis. We supported price control during the period of the war, as everyone else in this house supported it, at a time when the whole economy was controlled. We believe that price control can be made to function when the whole economy is controlled and regimented as it is or may be in some other countries. But we do not believe that prices of farm products cam be controlled by freezing them at the top and then letting costs of production go up; and we would mot be frank with the house, with the public or with our own convictions, if we said anything different.
I am going to bring at this time only two pieces of evidence with respect to the position we take. One of them comes from a report of a decision of what is perhaps the most realistic socialistic government of which we in this country are aware, namely the British government. The other is the position taken by one of the greatest and most enlightened organizations of workers on this continent, the American Federation of Labor.
First, I should like to read just three or four sentences from a radio speech by Matthew Halton, delivered two or three days ago. Speaking of conditions in the British isles, he said;
During the last ten days in Great Britain we've seen a political phenomenon. We've seen a Labour government pegging the level of wages, and Socialist M.P.'s asking for longer hours.
The next sentence is not essential, but I shall read it so that there will be no omission. He states;
If a Tory government had done this tliere'd have been uproar ini the country and probably a great wave of strikes.
Then he goes on to say:
In the last ten days Britain lias decided bo peg not only wages, but also profits, and the prices of all goods ini the shops. It's a drastic step in the fight for economic survival. Britain's fighting for her life; and1 the immediate enemy is inflation.
I have read that extract only because the British government., which we all respect, and with which we sympathize in its economic

problems, has said that it cannot control the cost of living by controlling prices alone, without controlling costs.
The other bit of evidence comes from the American Federation of Labor. I shall quote this brief extract from the monthly survey for January of that great labour organization;
Price control cannot dam ian ever-growing flood of money inflation. This has been proved again and again, in country after country. We must attack the root cause of inflation, the excess money supply.
We have had, Mr. Speaker, a long, interesting and, I am sure, informative debate on the speech from the throne. I arose only to say why we cannot support the amendment to the amendment. The only new light brought to bear , upon it was the experience of the socialist government in Great Britain where, to meet their problem, they have used not only price controls but wage controls as well. I have quoted, too, from one of the leading labour organizations in the vrorld, an extract in which it states that price controls alone will not cure the difficulty we are facing.
For these reasons we consider it necessary to vote against the amendment to the amendment.
Mr. MacINNIS; Before the leader of the opposition takes his seat, I should like to ask a question. In order that I might know, and so as to clarify my mind, do I understand that the leader of the opposition and his party are opposed to all price controls, rent controls and all those things?
Mr. BRA0KEN: I did not say anything of the kind.
Make clear what you are opposed to.
I am opposed-
Everybody wants to know what you stand for.

I am talking about the amendment to the amendment moved by the leader of the party to which the hon. member belongs. I am dealing with that, and dealing with that alone. That amendment to the amendment reads:
This house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to use the powers provided by parliament to control prices . . .
What I have said is this, that price controls alone, in an economy which is not fully controlled, will not accomplish even what my hon. friend wants it to accomplish. That is our view. His view is different.

I have produced two pieces of evidence to bear out my contention. One of them comes from the party which enjoys the respect and support of the hon. member and his friends; and the other is from the greatest labour organization on this continent.

I thank the hon. member
for answering my question. I understand that the Progressive Conservative party is opposed	
to all controls.

That may be the hon.
member's understanding; buh, if it is, then his understanding is very faulty.

I was paired with the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Farquhar) owing to the fact that he is ill. Had I voted, I would have supported the amendment to the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, now that the subamendment has been disposed of, there are certain observations which I should like to make. I am not completely oblivious of the mournful dirge we have had from quarters opposite, but I should like to remind hon. gentlemen over there that many of them have participated in this debate and a number of them have extolled the virtues of such a debate, laying particular emphasis upon the fact that it provides a general opportunity for all hon. members to participate, and it also points the way for bringing in of, and the consideration of, a wide variety of subjects. All I am doing now is taking advantage of the opportunity which they have reminded me is open to me.
It was just three months ago that hon. members first became acquainted with the contents of the speech from the throne. It is my earnest conviction that, had we been able to debate the speech in December we could have disposed of it upon that occasion. What we actually did was in my estimation utterly to waste a period of two weeks. No doubt those responsible for the procedure which was adopted on that occasion have learned a lesson, and undoubtedly there will be no recurrence of such a practice.
Much has taken place since last December 8. However, little has occurred to change certain convictions which I established in my own mind at that time. In fact, as a consequence of certain developments during the past three months, I am more thoroughly convinced than ever before of certain facts which I laid down at that time. Speaking in this house on December 9, the leader of this group (Mr. Low) asserted that there existed widespread dismay in Canada as a consequence of skyrocketing living costs. I should like to emphasize, and I believe it is quite clear to all, that, despite certain actions which have taken place since that time, one, the establishment of the prices committee, the developments have served only to heighten and intensify that feeeling of dismay to which he referred.
Only today it came to my attention through the medium of the press that the cost of living index has now' reached the very high figure of 150-1 points; that is, as of Febru-

ary 2, 1948. According to the dominion statistician, the increase in the index in the month of January was 1-8 points. It was pointed out in the reports that we are now just within half a point of the all-time high established during the so-called inflationary period following world war I. I should say, in passing, that this index is determined by using the base period 1935 to 1939 as 100.
A thought which has passed through my mind is this. Within a very few days, if not at the present time, the cost of living index will have exceeded the all-time high following the first world war. At that time what will certain hon. members opposite have to say, because frequently they have emphasized the fact that, even though conditions may be a bit bad, we have not yet reached the condition resulting from the Conservative party which was in power at the end of the first great war? There will be some red faces on the other side within a very very short time.
I cannot help but marvel at the way in w'hich certain government members rise to their feet and endeavour to varnish over so many things which are so completely obvious to the Canadian people. It is a sort of political clear varnish which our Canadian people are quite capable of seeing through. It is true, and I shall give credit where credit is due, that certain government members have been impressed by the general public reaction and have risen to their feet in this house and in a mild sort of way, it is true, criticized the government because of certain conditions which it has permitted to develop. The odd one of independent complexion, as it were, has displayed a bit more boldness in his criticism of government policy.
When the throne speech was debated in December the leader of this group emphasized that, among those who have been hit so hard because of prevailing conditions, are our old age pensioners and our widowed mothers. Can it be argued by anyone that these persons find the misery of their day-to-day existence any less severe than it was in December? In fact the figures which I have already given with respect to the increase in the cost of living would indicate that they are suffering much more at the present time than they did when the hon. member for Peace River was speaking. I would say further, respecting the aged, it is obvious that minor concessions, if concessions they were, of 1947 have already been gobbled up by the intensified whirlwind of cost increases. We recall that last year they did permit the single old age pension recipient to have a total income of, I belie re it was

The Address-Mr. Shmv
$625 a year; that is, including pension, and the married recipient to enjoy as it were a total income of $1,080 a year. On top of that I realize that there were quite a few thousands who were able to secure old age pension for the first time, but I am sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) would be the first to agree with me that these benefits acquired last year have completely disappeared as a consequence of the change in living costs.
Still struggling in this country and still hopeful, but rapidly losing hope, are those who have not yet reached the eligibility age. It need not be emphasized that one within this country must attain the age of seventy years before becoming eligible; but it is also becoming increasingly more obvious that those between sixty and seventy years of age are finding the struggle much more grim as each day passes. We have observed the number of persons within Canada drawing unemployment insurance benefits. We have examined the statistics indicating unemployment among able-bodied persons within Canada. How then can it be expected that those between sixty and seventy years of age are able to go out and compete in the labour market with the many physically fit unemployed today who are drawing the unemployment insurance benefits? In fact, among these persons we find a losing of faith, as I say, if faith they ever had.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch)
made reference to another class of persons to whom I had intended referring anyway, but I am glad he did. I should like to emphasize the point he made. I refer to non-pensionable medically-perhaps I should say physically-[DOT] disabled individuals. We have them within all age groups, persons who find it utterly impossible to leave home and search for employment, much less able to take such employment were it to be found. I suggest that those persons be eligible for the same pension that is made available to the blind today, because one who is totally incapacitated physically is certainly no better able even at the age of twenty-one years, to procure his living than is a blind person. Moreover, such persons should not be subjected to the humiliation of public relief.
During the last year I have received quite a number of personal and pitiful letters from such persons. True, they are proud. They worked during the years in which they could; but today, because of that incapacitation, they find themselves utterly deprived of the opportunity of procuring a living.
We have also laid stress upon the white-collar worker, the man in unorganized labour
who is witnessing an ever-shrinking pay cheque, with a corresponding decline in his living standards. His cry could well be, "How long,
0	Lord, how long." It is not a matter of doubt at all that within these groups we do find a great deal of hardship.
I should like to digress for a moment. I have referred to the disabled, and naturally the question of health comes to my mind. In dealing with health, I should like to refer to a newspaper report that appeared this afternoon. I am dealing with this because two years ago I had occasion to bring the same matter before the house, and, second, because the need within Canada of extended medical service is so great that every consideration must be given to an extension of these services. This article, appearing in the Journal of this afternoon, refers to the fact that refugee doctors are not eligible to enter Canada as such and are not recognized as being qualified either to practice medicine or to engage in surgery within the country.

turnover taxes and processing taxes, but which is certainly the most damaging of all. It has been emphasized that the government of Canada are siphoning off more than a billion dollars a year through these indirect taxes. They are taking money out of the pockets of old age pensioners, of the blind, of the incapacitated; they are taking it from the widowed mother and from the low-salaried worker, by virtue of the fact that these taxes are wrapped up in the prices of commodities these people must purchase. It is deadening as it applies to the consumer; there is no question about that. It is even worse when applied to the machinery which goes into industry as capital goods, because there you find it charged on the new price; you find it charged every time the machinery moves from one owner to another and, as I say, in its cumulative effect it is most deadening on industry. As the hon. member for Acadia pointed out, any deadening effect an action has upon industry retards the production which is so essential at this time.
I have gone back through the records of the late twenties and early thirties. I have read some of the Liberal speeches with respect to indirect taxes, specifically the sales tax. They were very proud of the fact that they had brought about this reduction and, believe me, they made it known to all the people of Canada. Then the Conservatives came into power in 1930, when times were a bit difficult. increase the sales tax from one per cent to four per cent and, as we sometimes say in a crude sort of way, the opposition, the Liberal party of that day endeavoured to take their hide off as a result.
